POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:49:56 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.12 EU rejects Trump’s case for new tariffs https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-rejects-donald-trump-case-for-new-tariffs/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:48:14 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9390069 BRUSSELS — The European Commission on Wednesday rejected Washington’s claim that Europe is fueling global industrial overcapacity, after the Trump administration proposed a 15% tariff on the 27-country bloc.

“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Olof Gill, the Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson, said in a statement. 

“The EU and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” he added. 

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, led by Jamieson Greer, found that 14 trading partners, including the European Union, China and Japan, had artificially deflated prices by flooding markets with manufactured goods. The decision follows a trade investigation launched in March.

Greer on Wednesday proposed a 15% tariff on the European Union, in line with the ceiling agreed in the transatlantic trade truce struck in July 2025 between U.S. President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

Greer, who is expected to dial in next Monday to a meeting of European trade ministers, can expect pushback on the excess capacity probe. EU ministers are also expected to bring up the lack of progress on lowering tariffs on EU products containing steel — some of which still face U.S. duties of as high as 50%.

The overcapacity investigation, launched under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, is the second of two trade probes initiated in the spring as part of the Trump administration’s mission to rebuild its tariff wall. 

After the “reciprocal” duties Trump imposed in 2025 were invalidated earlier this year by the U.S. Supreme Court, the administration imposed a 10% tariff on the European Union, citing concerns that Brussels had failed to ban the import of goods made using forced labor. The higher of the two tariff rates will apply, rather than the two being added together, a senior U.S. official said. 

The official added that the proposed duties would likely take effect in January at the earliest, after USTR holds hearings and receives public comments.

The chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, Bernd Lange, lambasted the conclusions of the USTR report as “absurd.”

]]> en Ukraine’s raid in Libya damaged more than a Russian warship https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-russia-warship-attack-libya-international-law-neutral-waters/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 25 Nov 2026 11:49:29 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9384750 Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO.

Ukraine’s attack on a Russian warship in a Libyan port was a striking military success. It may also have broken international law.

“An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war” was how Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauded Sunday’s sinking of the Merkury, one of Russia’s most advanced corvettes, docked at the time in Benghazi. Ukraine’s leader proudly announced on his Telegram channel that the operation, involving seven Ukrainian-made sea drones, had also disabled a Russian cargo ship suspected of transporting weapons.

From a military perspective the operation was indeed another one of Ukraine’s audacious commando missions. It was reminiscent of the derring-do spirit of Winston Churchill’s “Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare,” better known as the Special Operations Executive, which mounted commando raids along the French coast, causing havoc and raising British wartime morale during WWII .

In fact, the day before, while visiting Kyiv, Britain’s defense secretary Wes Streeting had coincidentally compared Zelenskyy to Britain’s iconic wartime leader.

The comparison was ironic given the circumstances. Despite Churchill’s impatience and determination to take the fight to the enemy, the wartime prime minister was careful to avoid breaching the laws of armed conflict at sea. He didn’t, for example, order British warships to sink the German cruiser Admiral Graf Spee when it was cornered in Montevideo after the Battle of the River Plate. The trapped warship’s captain ultimately decided to scuttle the ship.

But Zelenskyy wasn’t so restrained this week. According to international legal scholars, the attack likely violated international law as well as Libya’s sovereignty. The country’s eastern administration, based in Benghazi, has called on the U.N. to investigate the sinking as well as “reports regarding the presence of Ukrainian personnel, experts or military units” in western Libya.

The Libyans would have a good case if they lodged a complaint with the International Court of Justice, said David Letts, a retired Australian naval officer and now director of the military law program at the Australian National University in Canberra. “Unless you’re wanting to mount an argument that Libya is somehow involved in the conflict between Ukraine and Russia and neutrality doesn’t apply, I’m struggling to see how this sinking sits within the law,” Letts said.

Letts is one of the authors of the Newport Manual on the Law of Naval Warfare, a compilation of legislation published and updated by the U.S. Naval War College. He says Ukraine’s Benghazi attack is “quite different when compared to their strikes against Russian vessels in the Black Sea and in Black Sea ports” in disputed and not neutral waters.

The laws of neutrality are largely based on the 1907 Hague Convention, which codified the rights and duties of non-belligerent states during armed conflicts. Under it, countries at war are prohibited from conducting attacks, blockades or mine-laying within neutral waters. In return, neutral states shouldn’t let belligerent warships turn their ports into military bases. Stays are generally limited to 24 hours, with exceptions for damage, repairs or poor weather.

“The attack was a violation of Libya’s neutrality,” said James Kraska of the U.S. Naval War College and professor of international maritime law in the Stockton Center for International Law. “An attack is lawful if it’s beyond 12 nautical miles from the coastline, but, of course, inside it’s a violation.”

“Now on the Ukrainian side, what their argument might be is that a belligerent warship ought only to stay 24 hours in a foreign neutral port. If it goes beyond 24 hours, then the warship is at risk, and Libya might not be in compliance,” Kraska, a retired U.S. Navy commander, told POLITICO. “If there’s inclement weather, or repairs are needed to make it seaworthy, then the time can be extended,” he added. Some scholars, he added, would argue that Ukraine would need to contact the Libyan authorities to find out the status.

In terms of its boldness and reach, Monday’s attack wasn’t entirely unprecedented. In March, Libyan authorities reported damage to the Russian gas tanker Arctic Metagaz while it was en route to Egypt. Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the tanker with naval drones likely launched from Western Libya. Kyiv neither confirmed nor denied its involvement.

The governments of Sudan, Mali and Niger have also accused Ukrainian special forces of mounting operations in their countries, where Russian mercenary soldiers are present. Kyiv has denied those allegations.

This time, though, Kyiv has proudly admitted sinking the Merkury in a neutral port. Why? And does the breach of law on neutrality actually matter? Zelenskyy’s office didn’t respond to questions from POLITICO on the sinking, including as to whether it had sought counsel from senior government law officers before approving the attack, and whether it had notified Libyan authorities beforehand to request the ship leave Benghazi.

In the past, when questions of neutrality have arisen or Ukraine has been accused of breaching the laws of warfare, Kyiv has said this is no time for niceties as it is the aggrieved nation. When a U.N. monitoring mission in 2023 alleged abuse of Russian POWs, for example, the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry thanked the mission for documenting Russia’s violations but pushed back on the claims against Kyiv, arguing: “We consider it unacceptable to place responsibility on the victim of aggression.”

Former U.K. diplomat Tim Willasey-Wilsey, now a fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a defense think tank in London with close ties to Ukraine’s defense ministry, says that when it comes to the sinking of the Merkury, he doesn’t believe the legal issues are important. “Who gives a stuff, really, you know? To be honest, I don’t think the legality particularly matters.”

He said the biggest political risk for Kyiv is diminishing the “remarkable degree of Western support for Ukraine,” and so was reassured when Wes Streeting came out so quickly in support. The attack, he said, reflected desperation in Ukraine, where ballistic missile attacks are devastating civilian infrastructure, itself a violation by Russia of international law. “The war is clearly getting more and more visceral, and I think the timing of the Benghazi attack is testimony to the sense of desperation that there is now in Kyiv.”

But turning a blind eye to the Benghazi attack only adds to the erosion of international legal norms and the undermining of the post-1945 “rules-based international order,” which Moscow and Beijing have little time for. It makes the seas more dangerous.

Letts stressed how important it is for countries like Ukraine to stick to what’s legal. “I wonder what the attitude would be if this vessel had been docked in Genoa or Southampton, say, rather than Benghazi,” he added. “I think there’s an element here of ‘It was only over there, so it doesn’t really matter.’”

“Having built up a body of law that tries to protect victims of armed conflict, tries to limit the scope of armed conflicts, are we willing to wave goodbye to all of that?” he asked. “Are we willing just to have total warfare with all the rules gone and to say, ‘The last 100 years or so are a waste of time. Do whatever you want.’ I don’t think we are.”

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:03:55 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 Slovakia’s Fico snubbed Poland and Europe, insulted Ukraine veterans (again), and callously lied about Putin’s war (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,734) https://euobserver.com/251560/slovakias-fico-snubbed-poland-and-europe-insulted-ukraine-again-and-callously-lied-about-putins-war-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1734/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:03:32 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251560 As Slovak PM Robert Fico shrugs off war in Lviv and snubs both Warsaw and Brussels, thousands of grieving families, maimed soldiers and fresh Russian strikes in western Ukraine expose just how far his rhetoric has drifted from the front’s brutal reality.]]>
  • An attempt to explain to Slovakia’s prime minister that there is a war in Lviv.
  • The situation in Kupiansk is worsening.
  • New details about the disastrous Ukrainian attack on Toretsk last spring, and a comparison with the current situation.
  • Maps of the day – Kupiansk and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi; Toretsk in May 2025; Toretsk and Kostiantynivka in November 2026.
  • Videos of the day – Ukrainians received their first Lynx fighting vehicles and shared interesting details about them; the Russians captured Popasna on 7 May 2022, and today it is 40 km from the front line and a ghost town; a pickup truck is missing a wheel, so soldiers replaced it with a tree stump.

    • An attempt to explain to Slovakia’s prime minister that there is a war in Lviv. “There is simply not even a hint of any war in Lviv. The war there is concentrated primarily on the front line,” Robert Fico said on Wednesday (25 November) morning at the Slovak parliament’s European affairs committee, following his recent visit to Lviv, in Western Ukraine.

    He also reiterated to MPs that Slovakia would not support the €45bn loan for Ukraine. He described the European Commission’s effort to split it into two parts, with €25bn going to military aid and €20bn to civilian aid, as “a trick by the Commission”.

    Fico made these remarks just two days after Polish prime minister Donald Tusk called on him to show solidarity with Poland, whose territory was hit by Russian cruise missiles. “I do not know whether this appeal will touch your soul, but I am certain that this issue will determine Europe’s future,” Tusk said about aid to Ukraine.

    This is not the first time the Slovak prime minister has cast doubt on Ukraine’s suffering. While he himself has not yet dared to travel to Kyiv, on 23 January 2024 he nonetheless arrogantly declared: “Do you seriously think there is a war in Kyiv? Surely you cannot be serious. Life there is completely normal.” By then, the Ukrainian capital had already been targeted by air raids for two years.

    It cannot be assumed that Fico lacks the means to verify the real situation in Lviv, so the most likely explanation is that he is knowingly lying. Another possibility is that, under the influence of Russian propaganda, he has completely lost touch with reality. The following lines are an attempt to explain to the Slovak prime minister what city and what country he repeatedly insults with his remarks.

    ]]>         A Russian plan to federalise Moldova could give it a window to control access to EU membership https://euobserver.com/251069/a-russian-plan-to-federalise-moldova-could-give-it-a-window-to-control-access-to-eu-membership/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:45:15 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251069 A reported Russian plan to federalise Moldova would hand the Kremlin a lever over who joins the EU. Europe should rule it out before it reaches the table.]]> Moscow’s strategy in its negotiations with Ukraine is no secret. The war’s resolution is no longer the sole subject of bilateral talks, but rather one item in a long list of maximalist demands. Russia now demands a new “security architecture” for all of Europe, with the war’s end a secondary priority. 

    It is not hard to compare this stance with Russia’s December 2021 ultimatum, demanding that Nato members commit to no further enlargement of the alliance and a ban on Nato activity in Eastern Europe. Moldova, yet again, finds itself directly at the centre of Russia’s confrontation with the West. 

    In late November 2003, Vladimir Putin was preparing to fly to Chișinău to witness the signing of the Kozak Memorandum, a Russian plan to turn Moldova into an asymmetric federation in which the breakaway region of Transnistria would hold a blocking vote over national decisions. The plan collapsed the night before.

    Under heavy Western pressure, Moldova’s leadership withdrew its consent, and Putin never boarded the plane.

    Twenty-three years later, the same idea appears to be back. This time, the idea is subsumed within the negotiations over Ukraine. Europe risks watching from the corridor.

    Read more

    War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement

    Russian outlet Eho, citing sources close to the talks, reported this week that Moscow is seeking to restructure Moldova as a federation of Moldova, Transnistria and Gagauzia, with independence referendums in the two regions should Moldova join the European Union.

    The proposal would reportedly also include the withdrawal of Russian troops from Transnistria in exchange for a Moldovan commitment not to join any military alliance. The report is unconfirmed. But its logic fits Russian policy so closely that European capitals cannot afford to dismiss it.

    Read more

    [Interview] Moldova races for EU membership by 2030: ‘We owe this chance to Ukrainians’, minister says

    A veto over enlargement

    The most dangerous element is the referendum clause, because it targets the EU itself. Moldova’s 1994 law on Gagauzia already grants the region a right to external self-determination, if Moldova’s status as an independent state changes.

    The reported proposal would attach an explicit secession trigger to EU membership.

    If incorporated into a settlement, this provision would attach the threat of territorial fragmentation to Moldova’s European integration. The referendum need never take place for that threat to shape accession.

    Any Moldovan government would have to pursue membership knowing that it could trigger a new secession crisis. Moscow would gain a means of obstructing accession through Moldova’s internal politics.

    Russia’s economic leverage in Transnistria has weakened, with Gazprom’s direct supplies stopping in January 2025, while the EU accounted for 76.9 per cent of the region’s exports in the first half of 2026.

    A settlement of the kind reported would offer Moscow a means of converting that weakening material leverage into a lasting role in Moldova’s constitutional order. 

    Read more

    [Interview] ‘Whenever we take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies’. Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification

    Moscow has responded with escalating threats. Russia’s deputy foreign minister Mikhail Galuzin warned that Moscow would treat any attempt to force reunification as an act of war against Russia.

    More recently, Russia’s envoy to the OSCE claimed that Chișinău’s fiscal policy toward the region could provoke a new military confrontation. Moscow is treating the extension of Moldova’s fiscal rules as grounds for escalation.

    Gagauzia has no frozen conflict, no separatist army and no line of contact, despite latent tensions. Its inclusion extends the proposal beyond settling the Transnistrian conflict and into restructuring Moldova’s national decision-making.

    A federal settlement granting Moscow-aligned regional leaderships blocking powers over national decisions could extend Russian influence into Moldova’s central institutions.

    Read more

    EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe

    What Europe should do

    This is where Europe’s responsibility begins. Washington is in a hurry to close a deal, and a small candidate country on Europe’s periphery can look like a cheap concession from across the Atlantic. It is not cheap for the EU.

    The EU has opened accession negotiations with Moldova, committed €1.9bn through its Growth Plan and is now funding its air defences.

    All of that would be hollowed out by a settlement that hands Moscow a lever over Moldova’s constitution.

    Europe does not need a new policy, only to use the leverage it already has. First, the EU and its member states should state publicly that Moldova’s constitutional order and its accession path are not negotiable in any format without Moldova.

    Second, the mandate of Europe’s negotiator should include the full withdrawal of Russian troops and munitions as an unfulfilled Russian obligation. In May, the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas argued that Russian withdrawal from Transnistria should be one of the EU’s demands in negotiations with Moscow. That demand should be explicit in any European negotiating mandate. That promise should now be written down.

    Third, Europe should refuse any sanctions relief or return of Russian gas while Russian troops remain on the territory of an EU candidate. 

    Chișinău should turn its existing reintegration measures into a clearer political offer, with explicit guarantees for residents of the left bank, and Brussels should be ready to support it.

    It should put forward its own reintegration offer, with clear guarantees for residents of Transnistria within a unitary state, and Brussels should be ready to fund it. If there is no plan from Chișinău and Brussels on the table, it will consider one from Moscow.

    Paris-based NGO AI Forensics tracked four Italian Telegram communities circulating image-based sexual abuse material between September and November 2026, and found that these groups were quickly being replaced by others after they were found out.

    Invitation links for backup groups would remain pinned on the communities’ websites, which administrators prepared in case of a ban.

    In a report released on Wednesday (25 November), AI Forensics revealed that a third of the four groups’ messages engaged in seeking, offering, trading or selling intimate material depicting a real woman that is most likely known to the perpetrator. 

    Partners represented 12 percent of the groups’ targets, while five percent were acquaintances, 3.5 percent ex-partners, and 3.8 percent family members.

    Read more

    Women MEPs targeted by AI ‘nudifier’ apps push EU leaders to enforce December ban

    The revelations hit particularly hard following the ‘Mia moglie’ scandal, after an Italian Facebook group whose name translates to ‘my wife’ was found to be circulating images of 32.000 members’ partners and acquaintances in a swimsuit or nude without their knowledge.

    The subsequent response by authorities revealed a slow process that was easy to subvert by quickly disappearing and replacing groups.

    ]]>         Listen: Can the United States actually dismantle the International Criminal Court? https://euobserver.com/251436/listen-can-the-united-states-actually-dismantle-the-international-criminal-court/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 10:03:16 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251436 Tajikistan has officially announced that it wants to leave the International Criminal Court. This comes as Donald Trump steps up his campaign against the court, with Washington threatening sanctions and putting diplomatic pressure on its allies. So, how serious is the threat to the ICC?]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    Tajikistan has officially announced that it wants to leave the International Criminal Court (ICC). This comes as Donald Trump steps up his campaign against the court, with Washington threatening sanctions and putting diplomatic pressure on its allies. So, how serious is the threat to the ICC?

    Tajikistan was until now the only country in Central Asia to have ratified the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC. And it’s not the only country withdrawing. No fewer than six other countries have notified the UN of their intention to withdraw this year: Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, Chad and Nauru.

    Another blow to the court came last week, when Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping issued a joint declaration warning the court not to abuse its jurisdiction.

    Here’s a quick reminder of what the ICC is, and what it isn’t. The ICC was established in 2002. Its job is to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of four of the most serious international crimes: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.

    The ICC is a court of last resort. It is supposed to step in only when national authorities are unwilling or genuinely unable to investigate and prosecute these crimes themselves.

    Read more

    The clock is ticking: Europe is running out of time to save the International Criminal Court 

    That’s how it came to issue an arrest warrant against Russian president Vladimir Putin in March 2023 over the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.

    In November 2024, the court issued arrest warrants against Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant. They are accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, including using starvation as a method of warfare.

    Those warrants were made possible by the fact that the ICC can investigate crimes committed on the territory of a member state, even when the alleged perpetrators come from a country that has never accepted its authority.

    It can also exercise jurisdiction when the accused is a national of a member state, or when the UN Security Council refers a situation to it.

    Now, Washington wants to challenge that principle and, more broadly, dismantle the ICC.

    The US is seeking to prevent the ICC from exercising jurisdiction over individuals from countries that are not members of the court, even when the alleged crimes were committed on the territory of a member state.

    Such a change would fundamentally alter the court’s reach. On top of that, the Trump administration is also putting pressure on the ICC and its member states.

    According to Politico, US diplomats have been urging NATO allies to withdraw from the Rome Statute and immediately stop providing material support to the court.

    Read more

    International Criminal Court wins EU’s top human rights prize in defiance of Trump’s sanctions

    We cannot say whether the seven countries that have notified their withdrawal this year have done so because of US pressure. But the timing is noteworthy, particularly in the cases of Venezuela, Chad, Nauru and Tajikistan.

    And then, there are the sanctions. Over the past months, Washington has sanctioned several judges and prosecutors, including the court’s president, Tomoko Akane. In October this year, the United States went a step further and sanctioned the ICC as an institution.

    These sanctions have concrete consequences: restrictions on financial transactions, frozen assets, and bans on entering the United States, among other things.

    According to MEP Chloé Ridel, these sanctions are already affecting the ICC’s work: the prosecutor’s activities have slowed down, and some people have been sidelined from certain cases.

    But can the US actually dismantle the ICC? If fewer countries cooperate, the court becomes increasingly difficult to operate.

    The court still has 125 member states, and the withdrawal process takes time. But its ability to function depends heavily on international cooperation, financial resources and political support.

    The combination of American sanctions, diplomatic pressure and growing opposition from major powers is, however, sending a very negative signal about respect for international law.

    That’s why many actors are calling on the EU to activate its Blocking Statute, in order to neutralise the effects of US sanctions in Europe, at least.

    This would not be a game changer, but it could make the ICC’s work slightly easier if fewer companies were reluctant to work with the court because of the risk of US sanctions.

    So far, however, the commission has not proposed activating it.

German chancellor Friedrich Merz is demanding that all 27 member states contribute to Kyiv’s needs, while several countries are seeking opt-outs.]]> EU leaders are expected to clash on Thursday and Friday (26 and 27 November) over the latest proposal for the next EU budget, presented by EU Council president António Costa.

    Ukraine financing for 2027 is also set to be divisive – after German chancellor Friedrich Merz threatened to block the whole budget unless all 27 member states help pay for Kyiv’s needs.

    Costa’s revised “negotiating box,” unveiled last Saturday, cuts the overall size of the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028-2034 by €204bn in current prices, compared with the European Commission’s initial proposal of July 2025.

    It is also a further €40bn cut to the previous plan presented by the Irish presidency in early October.

    “On the MFF, the time has come to reach an agreement,” Costa said in his invitation letter to EU leaders on Tuesday (24 November), which also referred to the need to meet “Ukraine’s financing needs for 2027 … and beyond”.

    Costa said the EU has a collective “responsibility” to deliver a budget that could help the bloc deal with the challenges ahead, while keeping national contributions “reasonable”.

    To square that circle, he is relying heavily on new revenue sources, known in Brussels jargon as “own resources”, which he said could generate about €60bn a year.

    The main novelty is a digital tax, an old French idea backed by the European Parliament.

    Read more

    EU lawmakers target US Big Tech with budget-financing levy

    Other revenues would come from the Emissions Trading System (ETS), the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a levy on electronic waste and tobacco excise duties. On top of that, taxing crypto assets and earning revenue from radio spectrum auctions are also on the table.

    The problem with own resources is that they are a hard sell, because they are extra taxes that need unanimous backing from all EU member states.

    Costa’s proposal has already received criticism from the so-called frugal countries, including Austria, Denmark, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden, which believe it is still too high, and from the so-called cohesion friends, who say it is too low.

    Read more

    Costa’s EU budget plan for 10 percent cuts pits ‘frugals’ against ‘cohesion’ group ahead of crunch summit

    Sweden’s EU affairs minister, Jessica Rosencrantz, for example, said on Saturday that the budget remained too large and that Sweden’s contribution would rise far too much under the plan.

    Poland, for its part, leads the opposition to new EU own resources based on ETS, alongside Finland and the Czech Republic, and despite Costa’s proposal for a gradual phase-in from zero percent in 2028 to 30 percent by 2034.

    On Monday, the Visegrád Four (Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia) leaders, together with Austria, rejected Costa’s offer as “unacceptable” after a meeting in Bratislava.

    ]]>         [Interview] Cutting funds for Erasmus+ student scheme would be ‘giving up’ on Europe’s future, says lead MEP Zdrojewski https://euobserver.com/250689/interview-cutting-funds-for-erasmus-student-scheme-would-be-giving-up-on-europes-future-says-lead-mep-zdrojewski/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 08:34:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250689 Students need not fear deep cuts to the Erasmus+ exchange scheme in the next EU budget, despite the frugal winds blowing from member states, says Bogdan Zdrojewski, a Polish MEP who is the EU Parliament's lead negotiator on the programme.]]> As EU leaders gather in Brussels on Thursday and Friday (26 and 27 November) to discuss budget cuts for 2028 to 2034, even darling projects, such as the student-exchange programme, Erasmus+, risk losing out.

    The student scheme, which turns 40 this year, has helped over 17 million people to study and live outside their home country.

    Some 78 percent of participants say they improved their language skills and more than a quarter met their long-term partner during the exchange.

    But Polish centre-right MEP Bogdan Zdrojewski, who is in charge of negotiating Erasmus+ funding on behalf of the European Parliament, told EUobserver he remained optimistic despite the prevailingly frugal atmosphere.

    In your report of 22 October you outlined what Erasmus + should look like in the next financing cycle. Compared to what the European Commission proposed, you asked for an additional €7bn. How realistic do you consider this ask?

    We have to remember that we were starting with €26bn, which is the amount allocated for the current budget. It was important for us to increase that to account for inflation, including rising cost of living for students staying in different European cities.

    The most common demand was that we should take a more realistic approach to the differences in the cost of living between individual cities. We tried to demonstrate to the European Commission just how substantial the changes needed to be.

    We wanted to move away from a one-size-fits-all nominal amount and introduce greater flexibility. We also wanted that the situation would be monitored every year, possibly introducing adjustments.

    Another point is the overall budget. I was particularly keen to bring it up to around €50bn. NGOs and organisations working with young people suggested that it would be an appropriate response to the current needs.

    Read more

    Costa’s EU budget plan for 10 percent cuts pits ‘frugals’ against ‘cohesion’ group ahead of crunch summit

    ELIAMEP’s Seebass explained that the majority of the problems lay in the legislative and governance levels: “Even if you have legislation in place, it is often not implemented, and there is a lack of political will to implement these kinds of legislation, especially those for protecting the environment.” 

    Although she thinks that it can be an opportunity if it is taken seriously, with qualified people, high environmental standards and using the secondary raw materials, she admits that at the moment it is not. 

    “In examples such as the mine in Bor in Serbia, but also, for example, the chromium mining in Albania, you see that there is very little positive effect for the local population, since the costs are actually higher to the local population than the money that they make – and this is clearly a governance issue,” she said.

    “In Bosnia and Herzegovina, we see that local authorities are often the ones that are more interested in making money than to protect the people. About an hour from Sarajevo in Vares, there is an ongoing mining project and people are trying to get access to information on pollution levels, but they face a lot of opposition from the local authorities, including local council people, but also the companies themselves”, she added. 

    And while the protests in Serbia blew up to a massive scale, she found worrying that in Bosnia and Herzegovina some actors were exploiting existing ethnic and religious divisions in the region, deliberately fuelling tensions between communities to prevent them from uniting in opposition to mining projects.

    “People are just really fed up with not being asked”, Seebass said, adding: “We also see that there’s a lot of interest on the side of some governments to bring in money no matter what.”

    And that’s why Petković from Ne damo Jadar described the Jadar project as “a representative example of the collusion between a corrupt government, the corrupt capital of multinational corporations, and criminals.”

    Read more

    Green groups file complaint over EU water protection review, citing mining lobbying

    What now?

    The Jadar project is currently on hold, Petković explained. “The boreholes have been closed and rehabilitated, and the company says the project is in a care and maintenance phase. In general, the company has done nothing on the ground for more than five years that would advance the project, all it has done is maintain the boreholes, which it closed this year”, he said.  

    But despite saying that “strategic projects must also meet public acceptance obligations and demonstrate engagement with the local population”, the EU is sticking to its plans.

    “The Commission remains in contact with Rio Tinto to monitor the Jadar project”, a commission spokesperson wrote in a response to the Friedrich Ebert Foundation. “Both parties are working toward the implementation of the partnership”, they said.

    Parliamentary elections in Serbia on 25 October ended the 14-year rule of the Serbian Progressive Party led by Aleksandar Vučić.

    The Students’ List, a grassroots anti-corruption movement, won with absolute majority. The list is full of academics, professors, experts, and other prominent individuals from different fields, including agricultural activist Zlatko Kokanović from Ne damo Jadar. 

    Petković expects the new government to review every aspect of the mining project, to establish what was illegal in the way it was carried out, assess the damage caused by the exploration activities, trace the flow of money, and prosecute everyone responsible for pollution and fraud.

    “I expect Rio Tinto to pack up and leave Serbia, and the EU to stop insisting that the Jadar project go ahead and stop using it as leverage against the new government”, he said, referring to concern that Serbia’s accession to the EU now also depends on the development of the mine.

    ]]>         Sanchez’s snap election, and what his defeat would mean for Spain’s Nato spending https://euobserver.com/250954/sanchezs-snap-election-and-what-his-likely-defeat-means-forspains-nato-spending/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 10:22:33 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250954 Prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s rejection of Nato’s five-percent target was less hostile to rearmament than it looks. Military spending rose by 50 percent in 2025, and not even the election campaign slowed this pace down, as earlier this month the Spanish government authorised a further €12.2bn for air defence, counter-drone systems, submarines and ships.]]> Spain votes on Sunday (29 November), though its rejection of Nato’s five-percent target will probably survive a change of government.

    That reluctance is far from a rejection of rearmament itself: Spaniards are willing to spend more, but never alone.

    Prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s rejection of Nato’s five-percent target is less hostile to rearmament than it looks. Military spending rose by 50 percent in 2025, the steepest increase among the 15 biggest spenders, and passed two percent of GDP for the first time since 1994.

    Equipment purchases doubled, to almost €15bn, although under a rolled-over 2023 budget and with a 2025 plan that put only a fifth of its €10.5bn into new weapons.

    Not even the campaign has slowed this pace down, as on 10 November the government authorised a further €12.2bn for air defence, counter-drone systems, submarines and ships.

    Abroad, Spain leads Nato’s brigade in Slovakia, sent a frigate to protect Cyprus in March after drone attacks on the island, takes part in a new allied A400M fleet, co-develops the Eurodrone, co-founded the ballistic-missile-defence coalition and joined four of the five European defence projects of common interest.

    Spaniards would also rather pay through common European debt than through taxes or cuts, which makes Spain a testing ground for Europe.

    Where Spaniards agree

    This European faith partly reflects distrust of Donald Trump’s United States. According to an internal ECFR poll (see chart, 2026), 66% expect other Europeans to defend Spain and only 12% think Washington will. From Sumar (Greens/EFA and The Left), now part of the Frente Amplio (FA) coalition, to Vox (Patriots for Europe), every electorate gives net support to European weapons and a European nuclear deterrent. The US, by contrast, divides them, with 38% of Socialist voters (PSOE, S&D) seeing it as an adversary, compared with 8% of Partido Popular voters (PP, EPP). Common debt wins net support in every electorate except Sumar/FA, where it is tied, but putting a price on the national bill is enough to erode even conservative support.

    Sources: ECFR/YouGov (30 April–11 May 2026; n = 1,542; ±2.6 points) and survey data accessed by ECFR (13–19 August 2026; n = 1,638; tax question). Sumar: n = 67 and 62, before joining Frente Amplio (±12 points).

    Like most Germans and Italians, 54 percent reject cutting other spending to pay for defence, but for reasons of their own.

    Only seven percent see the US as an ally, and it is hard to sell a target that began as a demand from Trump. Spaniards also look south as much as east, and in May, before July’s Ceuta crisis, 67 percent already feared a migration crisis at Europe’s borders.

    What a new government would entail

    A change of government would alter the tone and the method, but probably not the figure.

    Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the Popular Party’s (PP) leader and candidate, signed up to the European People’s Party five-percent pledge the day after the Hague summit, but his party’s programme sets no GDP figure, and neither does the far-right Vox’s.

    The PP promises to honour its commitments with the endorsement of the Cortes, a multi-year defence law and joint European purchases, while its MEPs voted to explore defence bonds.

    Vox’s Santiago Abascal, for his part, has called for more money “to protect our borders and our interests”, starting with Ceuta and Melilla, and mocks a European army at von der Leyen’s “personal service”, even though his voters back the spirit of “buy European”.

    Under SAFE, the European Commission borrows on the markets and lends member states up to €150bn for defence, over the long term and at low cost.

    Nineteen countries applied; others, such as Germany or the Netherlands, which borrow more cheaply on their own, did not. It is credit, not a transfer, and it counts as national debt, so it holds little appeal for the most indebted.

    Spain is a case in point: it argued that it would reach two percent without straining its accounts and held off requesting the fiscal escape clause until April 2026.

    SAFE’s second call, opened on 29 October for the €21.3bn left unallocated, repeats the design, even though common debt has already funded the recovery fund’s grants and now sustains Ukraine, with €90bn agreed and a further €45bn proposed.

    Yet 53 percent of voters back common European debt for defence and only 28 percent oppose it.

    Going South?

    None of the five projects the EU approved in September looks south.

    Madrid should propose a southern-flank equivalent of Eastern Flank Watch, including the territories that Nato’s Article 6 does not expressly cover.

    With maritime surveillance, counter-drone defence and protection of critical infrastructure, it could be shared with Italy, Greece, Portugal and France and partly funded by the EU.

    The next government should also aim to join the E5, the group of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, which is committed to greater leadership within Nato and which, together with the EU institutions, forms the European team that will negotiate peace in Ukraine.

    To be sure, a European label should prevent any Spanish government from underinvesting at home.

    Nobody in Ankara accused Spain of failing to meet its commitments, but burden-sharing within Nato is moving against its budgetary position.

    Even so, Spain is proof that European rearmament wins over a public that rejects spending cuts and is divided over a purely national bill. Rest assured that Spaniards will rearm, but never alone.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/25/rise-energy-bills-britain-2166-impossible-high-millions-households-stocks-tumble-as-ai-rally-fizzles-live-updates</link>
      <description><p>New tariffs planned as Trump administration clamps down on ‘unfair trade practices’</p><p><strong>Hannah Webster</strong>, senior economist at the think tank <strong>New Economics Foundation</strong>, also called for other measures.</p><p>The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances.</p><p>The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out.</p><p>Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home.</p><p>Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator]<em> </em>has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/25/rise-energy-bills-britain-2166-impossible-high-millions-households-stocks-tumble-as-ai-rally-fizzles-live-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/25/consumer-prices-september-october-energy-inflation</link>
      <description><p>Rise occurs amid soaring energy prices, according to last inflation reading before a crucial Fed board meeting</p><p>Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, according to new inflation data released on Wednesday, the highest since May and the last <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/inflation">inflation</a> reading before a crucial US Federal Reserve board meeting next month.</p><p>Prices rose 0.3% from September to October amid soaring energy prices, according to the Personal Consumption Expenditure index, the Fed’s preferred inflation measure from the commerce department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/25/consumer-prices-september-october-energy-inflation">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/nvidia-staff-what-do-you-think-jensen-huang-return-chief-executive">Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?</a></p></li></ul><p>One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/23/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-nvidia-chief-executive">reinstated</a> Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.</p><p>But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jul/06/folarin-balogun-red-card-reversal-trump-calls-fifa-explainer">Folarin Balogun</a> after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer</link>
      <description><p>Amid air chaos, travelers will have to navigate an outdated system (and complex company policies if it all goes wrong)</p><p>Millions of people are planning to fly in the US over the Thanksgiving holiday, just two weeks after the US Federal Aviation Administration’s 13 November <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-ground-stop-flights-explained">ground stop</a> halted all flights nationwide for the first time since 9/11 (aside from a brief halt in 2023).</p><p>In the chaos that ensued, some travelers embarked on <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/royalcaribbean/comments/1xvkopq/comment/19smxjywidlcw/?context=3">overnight drives</a> to catch cruise ships and <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/women-stranded-faa-ground-stop-buy-ford-bronco-27-hour-road-trip-rcna609629">bought new cars</a> to make business meetings. Many had to simply cancel their plans and incur the costs that came with it. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled at a potential cost to travelers of $1.9bn in lost time and related expenses, <a href="https://www.andersoneconomicgroup.com/analysis-nationwide-ground-stop-cost-travelers-nearly-2-billion/">Anderson Economic Group estimates</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 25 Nov 2026 15:54:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Dublin publican Eamonn O’Malley behind The Yacht, Fagan’s and The Old Stand has died]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/dublin-publican-eamonn-omalley-behind-the-yacht-fagans-and-the-old-stand-has-died/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/dublin-publican-eamonn-omalley-behind-the-yacht-fagans-and-the-old-stand-has-died/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:49:40 +0000Well-known Dublin publican Eamonn O’Malley, whose family group owns a number of prominent pubs, has died.

The O’Mally Group operates Dublin pubs including Fagan’s, Drumcondra; The Old Stand on Exchequer Street; The Yacht in Clontarf; Cumiskey’s in Ashtown and The Autobahn in Glasnevin.

In 2025, the historic Dublin city-centre bar Peter’s Pub was acquired by members of the O’Malley family in a deal reported at around €5 million.

The pub subsequently returned to profit under the O’Malley Group, The Irish Times previously reported.

The premises had been run by Enda and Pauline Keogh for nearly 50 years prior to its sale.

Latest accounts for Peter’s Pub show it made a post-tax profit of €141,000 in the year that ended August 2025, compared to a loss of €713,000 in 2024.

The filings for Peter’s Pub Ltd show the venue is not linked to the O’Malley Pub Group’s main holding company Romont Ltd and is instead equally owned by Eamonn O’Malley jnr, David O’Malley and Sean O’Malley, who are aged between 30 and 34.

The family-owned group was founded by Eamonn and Michael O’Malley in 1990, with a primary headquarters in Drumcondra.

O’Malley died on Monday, November 24th, “suddenly but peacefully at his home”, according to an RIP.ie notice.

He is survived by his wife Carmel and sons Gary, David, Eamonn and Seán.

]]><![CDATA[US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/us-stocks-sell-off-deepens-as-ai-trade-cracks/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/us-stocks-sell-off-deepens-as-ai-trade-cracks/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:31:47 +0000A Wall Street sell-off intensified on Wednesday, pushing the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 down more than 4 per cent, as a brutal unwind of the once-dominant artificial intelligence (AI) trade accelerated.

Shares in Nvidia, which soared on Monday following the shock reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, slid as much as nine per cent. Rival chipmaker Broadcom lost seven per cent, while Micron was down 11 per cent.

“The mood is extremely skittish,” said Van Luu, director of global solutions strategy at Russell Investments.

The euphoria sparked by Huang’s return to the top job at Nvidia, America’s biggest chipmaker and the face of the AI boom, had been replaced by a growing realisation “that the scrutiny on the AI ecosystem will [now] intensify”, he added.

The falls briefly pushed the Nasdaq back into a bear market, defined as a fall of 20 per cent from a recent high.

Shares in Claude maker Anthropic, which fell below their $83 listing price for the first time on Tuesday, dropped another 9 per cent on Wednesday to just under $75 as the slump deepened.

Nvidia’s Jensen Huang apologises to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’

In early trading, Anthropic’s market valuation dipped below $1 trillion (€910 billion) for the first time since its listing.

The weakness in tech stocks extends a weeks-long sell-off as doubts mount over whether the historic AI-driven spending boom will pay off and how it will be financed amid climbing interest rates.

In a sign of the souring in risk appetite, traders bought into low-risk US government debt on Wednesday, pushing the 10-year bond yield down 0.08 percentage points to 4.82 per cent.

The Vix index of expected volatility, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, remained elevated at above 35 points, more than double its September low.

“It’s pretty wild out there at the moment,” said Jim Reid, global head of macro research at Deutsche Bank, saying the “risk-off” mood in markets was further stoked by the latest tariff headlines.

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday unveiled a number of new tariffs on major trading partners, including the EU, China, Japan and South Korea.

Donald Trump announces raft of new tariffs on major economies

The cracks in the AI trade also rattled Asian stock markets, with the region’s chipmakers suffering steep drops. South Korea’s Kospi fell 6 per cent while Japan’s tech-heavy Nikkei 225 fell 2.8 per cent.

Derek Halpenny, head of global markets research at MUFG, said: “The moves underline our view that the Jensen Huang return was a sideshow to the real issue undermining confidence: higher interest rates that are creating challenges for investors and undermining confidence in the sustainability of the financing structures in place that are driving the AI expansion.”

One US trader described the strong rally on Monday as “well overdone” and said there was “room to go” in the sell-off. “It does not feel like [investors] are done selling,” they said.

European stock markets, which are less exposed to the tech sector, were steady in afternoon trading, with the benchmark Stoxx Europe 600 down 0.5 per cent.

The region’s tech index was down 2 per cent and has fallen roughly 12 per cent in November, putting it on track for its worst month since 2022.

On the Kospi, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics – the two chipmakers that account for about half of the index’s market capitalisation – were down 11 per cent and 10 per cent, respectively.

The companies have been key beneficiaries of soaring demand for the memory chips needed in AI data centres.

“The dislocation in AI-related investments is global and specifically concentrated in AI infrastructure stocks,” said Sunil Garg, chief investment officer at Lighthouse Canton.

Wei Li, head of multi-asset investment at BNP Paribas Securities in China, warned it was “not a good time to buy the dip”. “The macro risk is just too high,” he said. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Demetrius Freeman<![CDATA[Donald Trump announces raft of new tariffs on major economies]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/donald-trump-announces-raft-of-new-tariffs-on-major-economies/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/donald-trump-announces-raft-of-new-tariffs-on-major-economies/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:23:20 +0000

Donald Trump has unveiled plans for new tariffs on the US’s major trading partners, including the European Union, doubling down on his signature economic policy despite steep Republican losses in the midterm elections.

US officials are proposing tariffs of up to 20 per cent on specific lists of goods from more than a dozen trading partners, with China and Vietnam facing the highest rate, and the EU being subject to 15 per cent.

The European Commission, which leads on trade policy for the EU bloc, said it expected new tariffs from the Trump administration to keep the total levy charged on EU goods capped at the 15 per cent rate agreed last year.

The 15 per cent “ceiling” on tariffs applied to trade from EU states into the US was “all-inclusive”, the commission’s trade spokesman Olof Gill said on Wednesday.

“We expect any measure from this investigation to respect it in full, including when combined with existing duties.”

The EU’s powerful executive arm rejected any suggestion Europe was a source of structural overcapacity, a concept in trade policy that describes a scenario where a country produces far more than its domestic market can consume, fuelling a need to export goods and products elsewhere, often at artificially low prices that undercut manufacturers in other markets.

“To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity. The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” Gill said.

Most of the new levies, which come after the US president’s “liberation day” tariffs were ruled unlawful earlier this year, will match the rates agreed in trade deals struck since he unleashed his trade war.

China had agreed a 10 per cent reciprocal tariff rate with the US earlier this year, on top of a 10 per cent levy that related to fentanyl. The new proposal for a matching 20 per cent rate could be doubled if US officials believe Beijing has stopped abiding by the terms of its previous trade truce with the US.

The latest wave of tariffs comes as Trump continues to push his trade strategy, even after voters punished Republicans in November’s midterm elections over rising prices, driven by tariffs and the war in Iran.

The US president’s top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, has been formally investigating a list of economies, including those of China, the EU, Japan and South Korea, over whether they give their own companies unfair subsidies.

Greer and other US officials have argued that government subsidies unfairly benefit foreign companies and harm US business, while also leading some countries to send artificially cheap goods to the US.

Earlier this summer, US officials applied 10 to 12.5 per cent blanket tariffs to trading partners to retaliate for failures to tackle forced labour practices. The new tariffs will not be added to those levies. A US official said countries would pay the higher of the two tariffs.

The proposed new duties will affect 14 US trading partners, including China, Japan, South Korea, the EU, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam, Bangladesh and Cambodia.

Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh all received proposed tariffs of 18 per cent.

Taiwan, Korea, and Japan will be hit with 15 per cent, and Singapore with 10 per cent.

Mexico and Norway were included in the probe, but reports on the two countries were not released this week.

A US official on Tuesday said for most countries investigated, USTR found that a “higher rate is warranted”, but it would be “willing to apply a lower tariff rate”.

The move comes a week after Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and less than two months before the ceasefire in the US-China trade war expires on January 10th.

The US official said Trump and Xi had a “great meeting” in the southern Chinese city and that he did not expect countries affected by the new proposed tariffs, including China, to retaliate against the measure.

US and Chinese negotiators extended their trade war truce by two months until January, rather than the much longer extension that Beijing had requested.

The US has been unwilling to agree to a longer extension because it believes China is not fulfilling its previous pledge to stop restricting the export of rare earths. The US official on Tuesday said the US had “seen some progress from them on rare earths over the past few days”, without providing details.

]]>Chip Somodevilla<![CDATA[Judge refuses to make orders following McKillen jnr complaint over reporting on insolvency deal]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/25/judge-refuses-to-make-orders-following-mckillen-jnr-complaint-over-reporting-on-insolvency-deal/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/25/judge-refuses-to-make-orders-following-mckillen-jnr-complaint-over-reporting-on-insolvency-deal/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 13:44:59 +0000A High Court judge has refused to make directions on foot of complaints by Paddy McKillen jnr over media reporting of his proposed personal insolvency arrangement.

Judge Nessa Cahill said publicity was a risk of the “substantial advantage” conferred on a debtor by the court’s insolvency process, and said she did not believe it was appropriate to make directions in respect of media reporting of the case.

Lawyers for McKillen jnr on Wednesday told the judge details of the proposed arrangement were reported last week by various news outlets, before the arrangement had been put before the court or placed on affidavit. They argued that this was not appropriate, and not in keeping with legislation underpinning the insolvency process.

McKillen jnr has told the court he has debts of €27.7 million and is insolvent. In September, the court granted him a protective certificate, which protects him from his creditors until at least December.

In the proposed personal insolvency arrangement circulated to McKillen jnr’s creditors last week − and reported by news outlets − creditors would have received €445,000, backed by €500,000 from the businessman’s brother Tyrone. Under that arrangement, McKillen jnr would keep a 1986 Porsche, a 1983 BMW and five paintings.

The court heard on Wednesday that that arrangement had been overtaken by an updated proposed deal, under which creditors would receive €1.2 million.

At the hearing on Wednesday, Martin Hayden, counsel for McKillen jnr, asked the court to direct that creditors confirm they had not published the complained-of material.

Hayden, appearing with Keith Farry, also sought a direction that there be no publication of material in the case prior to the “appropriate sequence of events”.

He said some creditors had not received the proposed arrangement by the time details of it emerged in the media.

He submitted the information received through the insolvency process should be used for the purposes of the proceedings, and not in “pre-emptive publication exercise”.

“It shouldn’t be that at every twist and turn there’s a media fest in circumstances where it’s difficult for all parties to deal with this matter,” he submitted.

Bernard Dunleavy, counsel for McKillen jnr creditor Herbert Street Property Finance, said there was no application formally before the court. He said he could not understand why McKillen jnr, and not the personal insolvency practitioner overseeing the process, was making the application.

Dunleavy, appearing with Niall Ó hUiginn, said he did not want to “ratchet up the temperature”, but submitted it was telling that the application was made in circumstances where the contents of McKillen jnr’s affidavits have previously appeared in news publications prior to that evidence being opened in court.

Aidan Redmond, for creditor Cabriz Finance, questioned why his client and Herbert Street were before the court.

Redmond, appearing with Martin Scanlon, said the two lenders were the only creditors written to in relation to the alleged leak to the media, and there was no confirmation the leak had not originated from McKillen jnr’s solicitors or the personal insolvency practitioner’s office.

His side had responded to the allegations, Redmond said, stating the proposed arrangement had not been leaked by his client.

The judge refused the application for directions.

She said the personal insolvency process is a public process that confers a substantial advantage on a debtor. She said the process carries a risk of publicity, a price that is paid for the advantage of a protective certificate.

She said she did not believe the court should be drawn into the matter, and said there was no basis for the directions sought.

Separately, the judge said she would issue judgment this week on an application by Herbert Street and Cabriz to cross-examine McKillen jnr on his financial affairs.

]]><![CDATA[The Christmas work party: What happens when things go wrong? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/25/the-work-christmas-party-are-employers-liable-for-mishaps-can-employees-face-disciplinary-action/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/25/the-work-christmas-party-are-employers-liable-for-mishaps-can-employees-face-disciplinary-action/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000The annual work Christmas party is both a beloved and dreaded affair, depending on who you ask.

Most staff members play ball and take part in the merry pleasantries, picking from canapes while nursing a beverage, and chatting to colleagues who up to that point had been enigmas.

Happily, the vast majority of work Christmas parties go according to plan, without issues, assaults or personal injury claims, although some readers might have tales they would take with them to the grave.

In advance of the Christmas party season, we asked experts what happens if things go wrong. Who is liable?

Can employees face consequences, including dismissal, for any wrongful actions at such an affair?

The simple answer is yes.

Employees appreciate the chance to let their hair down and connect with colleagues outside of their usual working environment, says Moira Grassick, chief operating officer at employment law and HR firm Peninsula Ireland. However, the combination of a relaxed atmosphere and the consumption of alcohol, some if not all of which is often free, can lead to “embarrassing moments, accidents, aggressive behaviour or even sexual misconduct”, she says.

Christmas parties are an extension of the workplace, Grassick says, “even if they take place off-site”, which means workplace policies and codes of conduct still apply, and employees can face disciplinary action if they breach those policies during the event.

Noting that employees might have different interpretations of “appropriate Christmas party behaviour”, Grassick says employers should issue a reminder of company policies ahead of time, saying they have a duty to ensure policies are communicated.

“We’ve all heard the nightmare tales of Christmas parties gone wrong, and it’s important for employers to mitigate risks where they can.

“It’s not a question of dampening the spirit of the event, but setting expectations early will help to ensure that no one wakes up the next day facing a disciplinary meeting as well as a hangover,” she says.

Grassick stresses HR professionals are “not the fun police”.

“We love a party as much as anyone, and the right preparations can allow for a festive party that is safe and enjoyable for everyone,” she says.

Jennifer Cashman, partner and head of employment at law firm RDJ, says an event organised, funded or endorsed by an employer can be regarded as an extension of the workplace, “even outside office hours”.

As such, employers can face liability for wrongful acts by employees during such events.

“Employers may have a defence where they prove they took the reasonably practicable steps required by legislation. Having a policy alone is insufficient. Communication, training and implementation matter.

“Importantly, conduct outside of the office can still lead to disciplinary action,” she says, including dismissal in serious cases.

Incidents after an official work event, including in hotel rooms or on the journey home, can also raise liability issues, she says.

My employer won’t let me carry over three days of leave to use in January. Is that allowed?

Employees can also bring personal injury claims against employers in the event of injury at Christmas parties, such as through falls, she says.

“Compensation is not automatic. The circumstances would need to be examined, including what caused the fall, who controlled the premises, whether a foreseeable risk was addressed and whether the employer took reasonably practicable precautions,” she says.

Cashman says risk assessments concerning the venue, equipment and employee needs should be undertaken. Like Grassick, she advises employers to remind employees that workplace policies continue to apply, regardless of the party venue.

“These should explain expected conduct, unacceptable behaviour, reporting procedures and possible disciplinary consequences,” she says.

Set finishing times, “sensible limits” on alcohol availability and non-alcoholic options are practical steps that can help events run smoothly, she says.

Asked if liability can extend to after-work drinks organised independently by employees, Cashman says employer liability is less likely where there is no employer knowledge, funding or involvement.

“However, this is not a blanket exemption, particularly for employment-related harassment,” she says.

In September, the then Minister for Culture and Communications Patrick O’Donovan told Coimisiún na Meán – in a letter sent before he stepped aside for the present due to ill health – that he was worried about ownership changes in the commercial radio sector.

In the letter, O’Donovan said he was strongly committed to ensuring that audiences had access to a diverse and vibrant media landscape.

“A vital part of this landscape is local commercial radio, which remains a highly trusted source of news for the communities it serves,” he said.

“I am concerned about the impact of ownership and organisational changes in the commercial radio sector at local and regional level and the impact this might have on the editorial and operational independence of stations and the local character of their programming.”

O’Donovan said it was essential that “the local character of these stations is maintained”.

He said in this context there would be merit “in paying particular attention to the plurality of ownership and content in the local radio sector in your next report”.

This report says a primary threat to media pluralism comes from concentrated ownership, and around a lack of transparency around ownership.

“This poses two main risks: first, the potential for a few dominant groups to control public opinion and influence democratic processes; and second, the possibility that editorial content could be shaped by owners’ interests or commercial pressures.”

“Of the 19 valid mergers notified to the Minister in this time period, eight mergers involved the acquisition of outlets in other countries, or the creation of a joint venture which would not be active in the State, which were reported to the Minister as the acquiring entities or the parties to the joint venture held media assets in the State.
