Russia has “categorically denied” that the three missiles which struck Poland last week were Russian and has accused Warsaw of seeking to “stoke anti-Russian sentiment” around the incident.

Its remarks came after Poland’s foreign ministry on Tuesday summoned Russia’s ambassador, Georgy Mikhno, to present him with a protest over the missiles. Today, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that expelling the ambassador is “one of the options” Poland could take, though it remains unlikely.

⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce

24 listopada 2026 r. JE Pan Gieorgij Michno, Ambasador Federacji Rosyjskiej w Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej, został zaproszony do MSZ kraju przyjmującego, gdzie przekazano mu protest w ramach rzekomego „powiązania” naszego kraju z incydentami… pic.twitter.com/GUJB0RWZgt

— Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) November 24, 2026

On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeastern Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border, amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. On Sunday, Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles.

Subsequently, on Monday night this week, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine and spent a few minutes above Poland before turning back into Ukraine.

On Tuesday, Mikhno was summoned to the Polish foreign ministry, which said it had presented him with “a very strong diplomatic note” regarding the missile strikes.

 

Afterwards, Mikhno read a statement to the media saying that “Russia categorically rejects the accusations of involvement in the incidents”, which were being made based on “political judgements and unsubstantiated assumptions”.

He also condemned what he said was “openly Russophobic rhetoric around the incident”, which suggests “a desire to exploit the situation to further stoke anti-Russian sentiment”.

The ambassador claimed that “no convincing and verifiable evidence has been presented” to establish the origin of the missiles. He then refused to answer journalists’ questions before leaving.

Russia has installed an exhibition titled “Ten Centuries of Polish Russophobia” outside a cemetery for thousands of Poles murdered by the Soviets in the 1940 Katyn massacre.

It opened just before Poland marked its annual day of remembrances for victims https://t.co/HcfmeNrerB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026

Mikhno’s claims were immediately rejected by the Polish foreign ministry’s spokesman, Maciej Wewiór, who said that it was “beyond dispute” that the missiles were Russian and that Moscow “knows [this] perfectly well”.

On Sunday, Polish prosecutors said that the remains of the missiles leave no doubt they are Russian, and added that preliminary findings even indicate which specific factory they were manufactured in and when.

A number of Poland’s NATO allies, as well as the alliance’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, have also condemned Russia over the missile incident and expressed solidarity with Warsaw.

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week.

Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026

On Wednesday morning, Sikorski was asked during an interview with Polskie Radio whether a “strong diplomatic note” was a strong enough response, given Russia’s repeated and continued hostile actions towards Poland.

When it was put to the foreign minister that Poland should expel the Russian ambassador, Sikorski said that “this is one option” and “of course, it can be done”. However, he added that “we won’t pursue it yet” and noted that any such action would be met with an equivalent response from Moscow.

In 2024 and 2025, Sikorski successively ordered Russia to close all of its consulates in Poland in response to Russian acts of sabotage. Moscow responded by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory.

🗣️ "Czy jest sens rozmawiania z ambasadorem Rosji? To symboliczny gest pokazania dezaprobaty. Liczą się sankcje i naciski gospodarcze. (…) Nie ma decyzji, by zerwać stosunki dyplomatyczne, ale one wiszą na cienkim włosku"

Rzecznik rządu @adamSzlapka w rozmowie z @Piekarski_M… pic.twitter.com/JU9up9cm5N

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 25, 2026

On Monday morning, Polish government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVP that “relations [with Russia] are hanging by a thread”.

He added that, while presenting a protest note to the Russian ambassador had been “a symbolic gesture of disapproval”, most important are “the sanctions and the pressure on Russia”.

“I think [this pressure] is strong from the entire European Union…[but] we’ve had doubts from the United States regarding these sanctions in recent months,” said Szłapka. “Poland believes [the pressure] should be consistent and stronger…I hope the entire Western world will be very clear on this.”

Poland and the United States have signed an agreement on defence research, development, testing and evaluation, concluding 17 years of negotiations and opening the way for deeper technological cooperation.

The agreement establishes a framework for joint defence projects, as well as the exchange of technical data and expertise, giving Poland – which is already a major importer of US arms – a formal role in the development of American defence technologies for the first time.

Under Secretary Emil Michael (@USWREMichael) and Mr. Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s Secretary of State at the Ministry of National Defence, signed the Agreement Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Poland for Defense Research,… pic.twitter.com/7EAgK3nD2i

— Department of War CTO (@DoWCTO) November 23, 2026

The agreement was signed at the Pentagon by Poland’s deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk and US under secretary of war for research and engineering Emil Michael.

According to the Department of War, the deal will help “turn research and development into validated military capabilities to jointly support US and Polish warfighters”.

Tomczyk said the agreement would allow Polish universities, research institutes and companies to participate in joint research and development work on defence technology with US partners and would enable such technologies to be tailored more closely to the requirements of the Polish armed forces.

During a briefing in Washington, Tomczyk admitted that the agreement had been negotiated for what he described as a “probably record-breaking” 17 years, but he noted a “significant acceleration in relations” between the US and Poland over the last six months.

 

General Marcin Górka, who oversees innovation in the Polish armed forces and accompanied Tomczyk to the United States, likewise welcomed the agreement, which he said would “open the doors to American military laboratories for our scientists and engineers”.

Górka also said the agreement would enable Poland and the United States to jointly develop anti-drone systems and advanced drones, with testing taking place in both countries.

Poland is a major importer of US military hardware. Between 2021 and 2025, it was the biggest overall importer of arms in NATO, with around 44% of that equipment coming from the US, including F-35 fighter jets, Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence systems and HIMARS rocket launchers.

But Poland has recently sought to move from being a client of the US defence industry to more of a partner. Earlier this month, Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed a declaration on expanding bilateral defence-industrial cooperation.

Poland and the US have signed a statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation.

Polish defence minister @KosiniakKamysz said his country would be "the US ambassador in the EU", including seeking EU funds for jointly produced equipment https://t.co/SKHrxTEKIW

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2026

Last month, Poland was chosen as the location for a planned Patriot missile maintenance and servicing facility, the first of its kind outside the United States. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks.

This year, Polish state defence group PGZ was chosen as the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles, while US defence giant Northrop Grumman and Polish arms manufacturer Niewiadów-PGM announced plans to jointly produce artillery shells in Poland.

Poland is also seeking to host a new permanent US military base, with Tomczyk reiterating during his Washington visit that a decision is expected from the Trump administration in early December.

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week.

Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026

The new agreement on defence technology was signed amid heightened tensions with Russia. On Friday, three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles struck separate locations in southeastern Poland, near the Ukrainian border.

Tomczyk said the Polish delegation had briefed Pentagon officials on the missile strikes, which he described as a “provocation” by Russia. The Polish minister was also asked about US President Donald Trump last week calling Russia’s Vladimir Putin his “friend”.

“One thing is certain: Vladimir Putin is not our friend; he is a threat to us,” replied Tomczyk. “This is the most important message that should come from Poland and resonate with the people of the United States.”

Subsequently, on Monday night, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine for a few minutes before turning back.

]]> Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated rights of migrants sent back to Belarus, finds European court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/24/poland-lithuania-and-latvia-violated-rights-of-migrants-sent-back-to-belarus-finds-european-court/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 15:03:07 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107447

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled.

However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders.

That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation.

📽️ Watch a video explainer on the Grand Chamber cases concerning instrumentalisation of migration.

📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur

— ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026

In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile.

In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus.

 

On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus.

The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had  “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”.

This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”.

Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention.

However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”.

That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus.

In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants.

A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence.

One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024

For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis.

The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus.

However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR.

The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation.

Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards.

They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025

In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”.

At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk.

However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention.

It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures.

⚖️ Grand Chamber cases

➡️ Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, European Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections.

🔗 Press release: https://t.co/nflEyCWKb1

— ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026

In response to today’s ruling on Poland, the deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Maciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”.

He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies.

The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration.

“In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC.

Bardzo ważny i dobry dla nas wyrok Europejskiego Trybunału Praw Człowieka.
Niezakwestionowano naszego modelu walki z nielegalną migracją.
Trybunał odniósł się do instrumentalizacji jako sprzecznej z Konwencją i podkreślił prawo państ do obrony i ochrony swoich granic.

— Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) November 24, 2026

A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards.

In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border.

Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted.

The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution.

The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%

Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026

Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration.

This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross.

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland in response to last week’s incident in which three Russian missiles struck Polish territory.

Shortly after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone that entered from Ukraine. However, although the military was given authorisation to shoot the object down, they did not do so after the drone began to move back into Ukraine.

Today, NATO Ambassadors met in the North Atlantic Council to discuss last week’s violations of Polish airspace. This was a dangerous incident and Russia bears full responsibility.
NATO and Allied assets reacted quickly to the airspace violations, and the Supreme Allied Commander…

— NATO Spokesperson (@NATOpress) November 23, 2026

On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeast Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine, and on Sunday Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles.

The missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before striking the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which were patrolling Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, received authorisation from NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre to fire upon the objects if certain conditions were met.

However, the pilots were unable to confirm their identity in time due to poor weather conditions.

 

On Monday, an extraordinary meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main decision-making body, took place to discuss the incident.

Afterwards, deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski, who represented Poland at the meeting, announced that NATO had agreed to place an AWACS “at Poland’s disposal”.

Later, NATO’s spokeswoman, Allison Hart, confirmed that “the Supreme Allied Commander Europe has authorised the forward deployment of a NATO AWACS aircraft” and is also “examining the deployment of additional assets as he continues to assess our deterrence and defence posture in Poland and elsewhere”.

Poland has confirmed that the three objects which struck its territory last Friday were all Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles.

Preliminary findings indicate the missiles were recently manufactured at a plant in Dubna, Russia https://t.co/4N6k3eBUGN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 23, 2026

“This is a very serious capability that gives us enhanced situational awareness,” said Zalewski, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. “This is an immediate NATO response, and we are very happy about it.”

“What I heard today is a great demonstration of the alliance’s unity with Poland in the face of Russian attacks,” he added. “It’s safe to say that the Russians have moved up the escalation ladder in their relations with NATO.This means…the need for an appropriate response.”

Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday.

Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment.

The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall.

“Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening.

“Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added.

The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express.

“The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper.

“We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added.

Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw

The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation.

 

The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking.

This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions.

The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope.

The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates.

Friday’s announcement brings to a close a process that was first announced in February and received European Commission approval in August. InPost’s shares have now been delisted from the stock exchange.

The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK.

A consortium of Advent, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF has completed its takeover of Poland's InPost, which is now private.

The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion.

In a statement published on Friday, Advent confirmed that InPost would retain its name, branding, Polish headquarters and operational independence following the takeover. Brzoska, who founded his business in 1999, will continue as CEO alongside the existing management team.

 

“InPost’s home market of Poland will remain the blueprint for new innovations, which will then be scaled across InPost’s wider European network,” said Advent.

They added that the new consortium would now “accelerate investment” in InPost’s operations, helping the firm “extend its reach further”. FedEx and InPost would also “explore opportunities” to cooperate with one another.

Brzoska, who is one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals, said that the new partnership would “deliver the long-term capital, global reach and deep technology expertise we require to build on what we have already achieved together as a leading European e-commerce enabler”.

While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation.

The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies.

 

On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism.

According to prosecutors, Nikita S., “acting on behalf of Russian intelligence and in order to obtain financial benefit of $500”, persuaded Dmytro Y. to “commit an act of sabotage by painting the slogans” with the aim of “publicly inciting hatred based on national differences between the Polish and Ukrainian peoples”.

The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP.

In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram.

When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities.

Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

Around a dozen monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the WWII Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).

Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia https://t.co/iaZb2CyiPx

Last week, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian suspected of carrying out the graffiti there and in Gdynia. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments.

The Ukrainian embassy in Poland has condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation” and “a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states”.

Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians.

Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases.

In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:52:11 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Poundland collapses into administration https://www.cityam.com/poundland-collapses-into-administration/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:52:03 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2483117

Poundland has collapsed into administration, it is understood, marking one of the highest-profile failures on Britain’s high streets in years.  Its owner, Gordon Brothers, had been in talks with multiple potential buyers for weeks but failed to find a new home for the discount retailer before a notice to appoint administrators came into effect. Poundland has collapsed into administration, it is understood, marking one of the highest-profile failures on Britain’s high streets in years. 

Its owner, Gordon Brothers, had been in talks with multiple potential buyers for weeks but failed to find a new home for the discount retailer before a notice to appoint administrators came into effect.

The US investment firm, which bought Poundland little more than a year ago, will now face intense scrutiny over whether it did enough to prevent the collapse, which puts the retailer’s 600 stores and near-12,000 employees at risk.

Gordon Brothers had been holding talks with multiple bidders in recent days: Irish property firm MPG, little-known investor Xyra Group Holdings, German-based Zachert Private Equity and Middle Eastern wholesaler Quality Premier Foods.

Any one of these buyers could still buy Poundland out of administration, though they had initially been attempting to buy the company as a going concern. The parties involved would not have let the retailer fall into administration if it was not confident that a sale of the company could still be possible after this point, people close to the matter told City AM.

Poundland’s management made the court filing on Wednesday, after initially filing the notice to appoint administrators late last month and extending it two weeks later, in a bid to buy extra time to find a new home for the retailer.

Gordon Brothers had rejected multiple bids from MPG over its insistence that it be repaid for a £30m loan attached to Poundland, of which it holds £22.5m. PepCo, the retailer’s former owner, had offered to defer repayment of its £7.5m chunk of this loan.

Xyra has been working with former BHS boss Tony Brown on its bid, which would have seen the retailer expand its store count in the UK and roll out more exclusive ranges in a bid to fatten its margins.

Zachert and Quality Premier Foods emerged as potential buyers later on in the process and have been holding talks with Gordon Brothers in recent days.

Gordon Brothers’s attempted sale of Poundland has been met with a political firestorm in recent weeks, as Westminster figures from across the spectrum accused the investment firm of prioritising its own returns over the retailer’s near-12,000 jobs.

Following a two-hour grilling in front of Parliament’s business select committee earlier this month Liam Byrne MP, its chair, accused Gordon Brothers of “jeopardising thousands of jobs on the British high street”.

Multiple people close to the hearing had said they suspected the investment firm always intended to let the retailer collapse, because it calculated that it could make more money by flogging its stores and estate to multiple buyers.

Poundland’s management and founder, Steve Smith, had also accused Gordon Brothers of blocking its access to vital funds needed to pay suppliers and keep its shelves stocked. The investment firm has denied these allegations.

A number of MPs are understood to be concerned by Gordon Brothers’s actions during recent months and plan to put the group under significant pressure once the discount retailer’s future is settled.

If none of the bidders in talks with Gordon Brothers are willing to buy Poundland out of administration, it will likely be broken up among a number of retail buyers. 


Tesco, B&M, Lidl, Iceland and The Range are among those who have expressed an interest in buying some Poundland stores. Administrators at AlixPartners would be in charge of running this break-up process.

Newcastle United’s owner, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, has hired JPMorgan to find a buyer for a minority stake in the club.

PIF is said to be willing to sell up to 25 per cent of the Magpies through a share issue, five years after buying the North-East outfit from Mike Ashley.

The funds are intended to be used for capital expenditure, with a redevelopment of St James’ Park or construction of a new stadium seen as the priority.

It is the latest example of PIF’s reluctance to sign off additional investment in sporting properties, after it pulled the plug on LIV Golf this year.

The sovereign wealth fund is also seeking investment in its Saudi Pro League teams and has cancelled high-profile tennis and snooker tournaments on home soil.

PIF initially poured extra money into turning Newcastle into a top six Premier League team following their £300m takeover in October 2021.

But tighter spending rules and restrictions on sponsorships from other PIF-linked companies have hamstrung their efforts to consistently challenge at the top of the table.

Newcastle the latest Premier League club to test market

As City AM reported this week, Newcastle have continued to bleed money through consultancy fees while they weighed up whether to redevelop or relocate.

In the meantime they have had to sell some of their biggest names, with Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon and Bruno Guimaraes all offloaded in the summer.

A share issue will see PIF’s roughly 85 per cent stake in Newcastle diluted. The Reuben family, which owns the remaining shares, could also be diluted.

It is not clear what valuation PIF and its advisors have set for Newcastle but Premier League clubs have been encouraged to test investor appetite by market trends.

The sale of a large minority stake in Liverpool that valued the club at £5.5bn was the latest in a series of transactions to illustrate the rapid rise in sports team values.

Crystal Palace appointed the Raine Group earlier this season to tap the market for investment or a full sale at a valuation of £900m. 

]]> 2483169Frank Dalleres Frank Dalleres Minister says young women ‘should not be left alone with an adult’ at work https://www.cityam.com/minister-says-young-women-should-not-be-left-alone-with-an-adult-at-work/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:30:53 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2483023

Businesses are facing a faster-than-expected ban on the misuse of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) and fresh calls for tougher safeguarding standards, as the UK government responds to a string of high-profile sexual assault cases. On Wednesday the Minister for Women and Equalities, Bridget Phillipson, said young women should not be left alone behind closed doors with [...]]]>

Businesses are facing a faster-than-expected ban on the misuse of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) and fresh calls for tougher safeguarding standards, as the UK government responds to a string of high-profile sexual assault cases.

On Wednesday the Minister for Women and Equalities, Bridget Phillipson, said young women should not be left alone behind closed doors with an adult at work, calling it contrary to basic safeguarding. Although she did not specify an age limit for this supervision, she framed it as a cultural standard employers should adopt alongside new legislation.

The government is bringing forward to January legislation to ban the misuse of NDAs in cases of harassment or discrimination, a policy previously scheduled for the back end of 2027.

Andy Burnham has called recent high-profile rape trials, including that of Russell Brand, who was found guilty earlier this month of rape and sexual assault, a “watershed moment” for the UK.

Labour added restrictions on NDAs to the Employment Rights Act, preventing employers from using gagging orders to silence victims of abuse, harassment, or discrimination. But along with Brand, the debate about NDAs has been reopened in the wake of allegations against David Walliams regarding inappropriate behaviour, which he has denied.

The Prime Minsiter credited high-profile rape trials as the reason the plans have been brought forward. Writing in the Guardian, Burnham said: “We’ll only stop the violence when we end the silence. It’s time for us all to speak up.”

He promised the move was “just the start” of a crackdown, and also pledged further measures next year to ensure freelancers and fans are also protected from gagging clauses.

‘Blanket approach’ risks backfiring

Changes to the use of NDAs has sparked debate in the City.

“There is entirely justified concern about the misuse of NDAs in cases of sexual misconduct and abuse,” said Philip Gardner, of counsel at Peters & Peters, though he warned a “blanket approach” can be “misconceived”.

Lawyers have warned the changes may make it harder to settle disputes, leading to more costly litigation for both businesses and victims. 

“Without the prospect of confidentiality, some employers may be less willing to settle, particularly where their investigation has not upheld a complaint,” Caroline Noblet, partner at Brian Cave Leighton Paisner (BCLP), said. 

“They may instead see a public tribunal judgment as the best way to defend their reputation. That could mean fewer settlements and more litigation, bringing additional cost, delay and stress for both sides,” she added.

Noblet said the changes are “a welcome objective”, but accelerating them while the consultation response remains unpublished “leaves businesses unclear about what exceptions will apply.” 

Beth Hale, partner at CM Murray, said it is not clear from the announcement “whether the government is now proposing a total ban on NDAs in cases where allegations of discrimination and harassment have been raised, with no exceptions.” 

]]> 2483023 Maria Ward-Brennan Maria Ward-Brennan City’s reliance on AI giants sparks sovereignty warning https://www.cityam.com/citys-reliance-on-ai-giants-sparks-sovereignty-warning/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:53:02 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2483003

Britain’s financial services companies are becoming increasingly dependent on third-party AI providers, prompting warnings over the City’s exposure to overseas tech suppliers and geopolitical shocks. Third parties now supply more than half of financial firms’ most critical AI systems, up from around a third in 2024, according to a techUK report published on Wednesday. The [...]]]>

Britain’s financial services companies are becoming increasingly dependent on third-party AI providers, prompting warnings over the City’s exposure to overseas tech suppliers and geopolitical shocks.

Third parties now supply more than half of financial firms’ most critical AI systems, up from around a third in 2024, according to a techUK report published on Wednesday.

The report warned that relying on multiple suppliers does not necessarily protect financial institutions from disruption, particularly when those providers are subject to the same country’s laws.

It pointed to US export controls introduced in June, which resulted in a leading AI model being suspended worldwide for almost three weeks, including for British customers.

The industry body also warned that lengthy and costly due diligence processes were making it difficult for financial institutions to switch providers, strengthening the grip of established tech giants and creating barriers for smaller British competitors.

“UK financial services firms don’t need to own every layer of their technology to be sovereign,” said James Challinor, head of financial services at techUK.

“What matters is having real control over the technology they rely on, the freedom to switch providers and a plan to keep critical services running.”

The report called for standardised AI contracts, including advance notice when models are withdrawn, and shared assurance schemes to prevent suppliers from having to undergo separate evaluations for every financial institution.

It also urged firms to establish contingency plans for their most critical AI systems rather than imposing blanket requirements to use multiple suppliers.

Lloyds Banking Group was singled out as an example of good practice, having developed an internal platform allowing developers to switch between AI models based on performance, cost and risk.

UK sovereignty ambitions

Speaking at techUK’s summit on Wednesday, City minister Lucy Rigby acknowledged the need to reduce critical dependencies across financial services, including on cloud computing providers.”We want UK businesses to have access to the most advanced technologies in the world. We must also ensure they have a genuine choice over the technology that they use,” she said.

The report comes less than a week after AI minister Kanishka Narayan said Britain did not need to develop its own frontier AI model, provided it maintained “trusted interdependence and access” to technology developed by allies.

However, techUK warned that insufficient domestic investment risked leaving promising British technology firms vulnerable to overseas acquisitions before they could become credible competitors to global providers.

The body called on ministers to unlock more long-term domestic capital for British growth companies, without mandating where pension funds invest.

Britain’s AI assurance industry contributed an estimated £1.01bn to the economy in 2024, according to figures cited in the report, with the potential to reach more than £18.8bn by 2035 if barriers to adoption are addressed.

]]> 2483003Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Burnham says EU deal ‘removed threat’ of Made in Europe scheme in clash with Badenoch https://www.cityam.com/burnham-says-eu-deal-removed-threat-of-made-in-europe-scheme-in-clash-with-badenoch/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:33:58 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2483077

Andy Burnham has said his deal with the European Union “removed the threat” of UK carmakers being hit by the protectionist ‘Made in Europe’ policy even as the government refused to confirm that a deal had been signed off.  Last week, Burnham’s reset deal with the EU came under question over firms’ access to European [...]]]>

Andy Burnham has said his deal with the European Union “removed the threat” of UK carmakers being hit by the protectionist ‘Made in Europe’ policy even as the government refused to confirm that a deal had been signed off. 

Last week, Burnham’s reset deal with the EU came under question over firms’ access to European markets and negotiations over tuition fees after European officials suggested alignments on food standards and carbon emission trading depended on students’ university charges. 

But in a heated parliamentary debate with Tory leader Kemi Badenoch in Prime Minister’s Questions, Burnham said the wider deal with the EU was not tied up by negotiations on tuition fees while British firms would not be impacted by the bloc’s ‘Made in Europe’ scheme. 

He said the UK had “got a deal which removed the threat from ‘Made in Europe’ from the British car industry, from the British steel industry, [and] from the aluminium industry”. 

The Made in Europe scheme attempts to protect EU manufacturing and supply from overseas competition by imposing ‘buy European’ rules for public contracts and increasing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. 

Businesses have pushed the government to ensure UK manufacturers are included in the scheme.

A spokesman for the Prime Minister later refused to confirm that a deal had been agreed, arguing there had been “positive engagement” with European counterparts. 

During the session, Burnham also said that talks on tuition fees were on a “separate piece of paper” to the main deal. 

When he was asked whether he could rule out EU students paying the same tuition fees as British students, he said: “That has not been put on the table; it won’t be put on the table.”

Burnham gets in a twist over EU talks

Mixed messaging over Burnham’s talks with the EU has cast a shadow over his push to bring closer ties and open the door to rejoining the bloc. 

Badenoch hit out at Burnham for not clarifying whether British students would have to pay higher fees as a result of lower fees apparently being offered to European students. The Prime Minister said the Tories should back “measures to boost growth” and that details in the wider detail were “in the British national interest”. 

Rows over EU ties have reestablished old political divides, with Reform UK leader Nigel Farage hitting out at Burnham for raising the prospect of a “divisive” second referendum. 

Burnham said on Monday it would be “unthinkable” to propose a return without giving the public the chance to vote directly on the matter. 

Influencer battles

During Prime Minister’s Questions, Burnham also came under fire over a reception held for influencers in Number 10 Downing Street. 

One content creator published a video with lewd remarks outside Number 10, which was later taken down. Other videos were filmed inside the building, raising suspicions over content creators’ relationships with the government. Influencers have been paid millions of pounds by government departments for advertising and highlighting government initiatives. 

In the Commons, Badenoch urged Burnham to “apologise for debasing his office” and allowing obscene language to be used outside Number 10. 

Burnham refused to apologise directly as he said the video was “inappropriate” and “unacceptable”.

[Badenoch] sneers at TikTokers, she sneers at influencers.,” Burnham said. “Young people are looking to these people for their information.”

“We’re giving people hope, and we won’t be distracted by her negativity.”

The blockbuster fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury has been given the go-ahead by Cardiff councillors despite concerns that it could spark “absolute chaos”.

Joshua and Fury are set to clash at the city’s Principality Stadium next month in a bout not set to begin until 1:30am in order to satisfy the demands of US broadcasters.

That required an extension of the venue’s licensing hours from 1am to 3am, which was granted at a meeting of Cardiff Council’s licensing sub-committee on Wednesday.

Preventing cyberattacks should be seen as fundamentally an economic as well as a technical problem, writes Paul Ormerod

Cybersecurity used to be something only nerds and geeks had heard about. Now, it seems hardly a day passes without some new attack being featured in the media.

In March, for example, a vulnerability in Companies House’s Web Filing service left the personal data of company directors across 5m registered UK businesses accessible to anyone with a login. Last month, online fashion retailer ASOS confirmed a breach exposing customer names and contact details. Companies this year have still been dealing with the aftermath of major attacks in 2025 such as the one on Jaguar Land Rover.

A government survey estimates that 69 per cent of large businesses experienced a breach or attack over the past year. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) suggests that malicious cyber activity costs businesses some £15bn a year.

Cybersecurity is an economics problem

The problem is often seen as being essentially a technical one. Technology, and increasingly AI, causes the issues, so technology and AI should be used as the main line of defence.

It is obvious that technology has to be used. But this simply sets up a classic evolutionary game, in which both attackers and defenders are constantly changing and developing their strategies. There is no guarantee that the good guy wins. Their generative AI-developed tool will quite frequently be better than yours.

A paper just published by top Stanford economist Susan Athey and colleagues in the leading Journal of Economic Perspectives offers a different perspective. They argue that cybersecurity is fundamentally an economic as well as a technical problem. Bringing the economics in provides an additional level of defence.

Modern economies rely heavily on a small number of digital platforms, software products and technology providers. When vulnerabilities emerge in these concentrated systems, failures can affect thousands of organisations simultaneously, creating systemic cyber risk analogous to systemic risk in finance.

Regulation isn’t a silver bullet against cyberattacks

Athey and colleagues are very sceptical of highly prescriptive conventional compliance-based regulation, the immediate tool for which many policymakers instinctively reach.

Regulators typically specify a long checklist of requirements. But technology and attack methods change faster than the regulatory process.

The authors explicitly worry that EU-style detailed regulation can consume resources negotiating rules and compliance procedures without knowing whether the requirements actually generate commensurate security benefits. Further, it can so easily degenerate into a tick-box exercise in which the main aim is to satisfy the regulator rather than solve the problem.

But neither are markets

But they are also not enamoured of a much more market-based approach. Several factors mean that firms will usually under-invest in cyber security.

For example, the firm itself rarely bears the full cost of incidents, which often fall on customers and other organisations rather than the provider. In the jargon of economics, this is a negative externality. The classic example is the factory which pollutes the neighbourhood.  

Remarkably, a problem is also created by the very opposite effect, namely positive externalities. My security investment can make you safer, so there is always an incentive for you to free ride on my cybersecurity spend.

They do not pretend to have a silver bullet. But Athey and colleagues, both of whom are cyber experts, make several interesting suggestions.

They do not dismiss regulation but argue that it should be pruned to focus on the rules which produce greatest benefit relative to cost. Government should increase substantially the amount of information it provides on matters such as which products work best.  

They advocate much greater sharing by companies, through sector-specific Information Sharing and Analysis Centres and disclosure to government regulators, with commercially sensitive information protected. And given that the market will underprovide, subsidies for cyber investment are needed.

The main point is a simple one. Technology alone will not defeat cybercrime. Incentives have a key role to play.

Paul Ormerod is an honorary professor at the Alliance Business School at the University of Manchester. You can follow him on Instagram @profpaulormerod

Around £660m was stolen in the first six months of 2026, according to new figures from trade body UK Finance, driven by a surge in authorised push payment (APP) fraud. This type of fraud occurs when a scammer tricks a customer into sending money directly, typically under false pretences or high pressure.

These cases accounted for £316m in losses, 22 per cent higher year-on-year. APP cases also rose by a quarter to 138,345.

Total fraud rose eight per cent, despite overall cases dropping 14 per cent to over 1.7m.

Investment scams were the largest driver of financial loss at £126m, accounting for 40 per cent of all APP losses, with an average loss of £16,000 per case. AI enhancing fraud threats

UK Finance said criminals can “enhance” traditional fraud measures with “artificial intelligence tools and more sophisticated social engineering techniques”.

Banks have stepped up security and governance over the last year to combat growing AI-driven threats to cybersecurity and fraud.

“AI is giving criminals the ability to create increasingly convincing content and social engineering at scale, making it harder for consumers to distinguish legitimate communications from fraud,” Erin Sims, financial services senior analyst at RSM UK, said.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has called on social media giants to take greater responsibility for online scams following the rapid spread of AI-generated content.

Speaking at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting, Bailey said: “We must get the social media companies involved because a lot of this fraud goes through those channels… There is responsibility all round because this cannot be done by finance alone.”

A judge threw out the UK government’s bid to disqualify the founder and former chairman of a collapsed property development firm over allegations he knowingly breached rules to secure £400,000 in Covid-era business loans.

The government’s business department filed a disqualification order against Gary Forrest, of the High Street Group, known for constructing Newcastle’s tallest building, Hadrian’s Tower, after the firm and its eight subsidiaries entered administration and were liquidated.

In May 2020, Forrest had applied for and secured the loans, valued at £50,000 each, under the government-backed Bounce Back Loan (BBL) scheme for businesses during the pandemic, which permitted only one loan per corporate group.

In a judgment handed down on Tuesday, deputy insolvency judge Stephen Baister ruled that while Forrest had breached the rules in securing the loans, the Insolvency Service failed to prove Forrest “knew, or ought to have known” he was breaking the rules, which the government had argued.

Judge Baister said that when concluding whether Forrest “had actual knowledge” of the terms of the loan scheme he was claimed to have breached, the judge had “little difficulty in concluding that he did not” have that knowledge.

The judge, referring to the Insolvency Service’s argument, said there “is no evidence that he was given or otherwise put on notice of the terms of the BBL scheme which, as I have already observed, are not in evidence.”

‘Cavalier’ approach to loan applications

The judge said Forrest “was cavalier (even reckless)” in his approach to the loan applications, but that it “was a mistake.”

“It amounted to incompetence but not to incompetence to the marked degree necessary to make him unfit to be a director and warrant making a disqualification order,” Baister said.

“Critically, the court held that Mr Forrest neither knew, nor ought to have known, that the companies who applied for the Bounce Back Loans were breaching the terms of the Bounce Back Loan Scheme,” Vivienne Burbidge, partner at Orwins, who represented Forrest in the proceedings, told City AM.

“He made a mistake, but his conduct was not such as to make him unfit to be a director and warrant making a disqualification order,” she said, adding that “very few disqualification cases are successfully defended.”

A spokesperson for the Insolvency Service said in a statement on the ruling: “We note the court’s judgment and have nothing further to add at this point.”

Over £200m of debt left behind

The High Street Group plunged into administration in 2021, but was wound up in August 2024 after administrators could not recover any funds for creditors.

According to Companies House filings from 2024, the firm left behind an estimated £212m in debts, including £123.5m owed to secured loan note investors and nearly £1m to HMRC for overdue PAYE payments.

Administrators reported in the filings that they had recovered no assets, leaving creditors facing total losses.

City AM revealed in April 2024 that the Insolvency Service has successfully disqualified over 800 directors for misusing the loan scheme.

When KPMG spun out its restructuring business to HIG Capital in 2021, former chief executive Blair Nimmo said the deal signalled a new era of growth for the unit outside the Big Four umbrella.

“From the strong foundations that we’ve built over the past 50 years, we’re looking forward to building a market-leading international advisory business that is capable of servicing the largest and most complex engagements,” Nimmo said.

But five years on, Interpath is at a crossroads. Despite posting revenue of £250m, the spin-out, now on its second private equity owner, has been rocked by senior departures and reported executive clashes. 

Industry sources told City AM the firm has not had “a clear view” since KPMG sold it. While it has diversified, the company has struggled to shake off its reputation as an administrator, compared to competitors such as Alvarez & Marsal and Alix Partners, the people said. 

On Wednesday, the group reported revenue for the year ended 3 April 2026 climbed to £250m, up from £198.1m a year earlier. Pre-tax earnings rose nearly 28 per cent to £74.9m. 

Interpath said it sees strong trading in the first half of 2027, putting it on course to approach £300m in net revenue by March 2027. Unlike its previous result announcements, the firm did not disclose statutory operating profit, headcount, or revenue splits between its restructuring and advisory arms. 

Building a global footprint

Interpath Advisory was formed in 2021 with backing from US private equity giant HIG Capital after KPMG spun it out in a deal roughly valued at £400m. 

At the time of the carve-out, approximately 538 staff and 22 partners transferred to Interpath. 

Since 2021, the firm has expanded globally from a UK-focused restructuring carve-out firm to 30 locations. It acquired KPMG France’s restructuring business for £5.5m in cash, Kerkhoff Group, a German-Austrian supply chain advisory firm, for £7.5m, and Balto in Spain in May 2025.

In the 2026 financial year, Interpath launched in Switzerland, Hong Kong, and South Africa. 

On Wednesday, the group chief executive, Mark Raddan, confirmed the firm was also exploring a deal to buy a US firm with about 200 people, which it plans to use as a launchpad for further expansion.

Since the spin-out, and as a result of its expansion, its global headcount has grown to over 1,100 people, including more than 100 managing directors.

In January, it was reported that Interpath Holdings, the parent group entity, reported revenue rising over 26 per cent to £198.1m for the 12 months to 28 March 2025, but expansion-related non-underlying costs of £31.7m and finance costs of £25.6m pushed the group to a net loss of nearly £10m.

Exit of the rainmakers

Bridgepoint recently completed a £800m majority-stake takeover of Interpath from HIG Capital, the private equity firm that initially bought the former Big Four arm. 

This comes as the firm faces potential revenue squeeze following the reported departure of six senior restructuring directors, including UK chief executive Will Wright, who reportedly helped generate roughly £30m of the firm’s £123m restructuring revenue in 2025.

According to Companies House, Wright resigned as Interpath director on 2 July. Reports said this followed months of tension between him and Interpath’s global chief executive, Mark Raddan, after the Bridgepoint deal. 

In August, the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW) fined Raddan £8,000 and reprimanded him for two breaches of confidentiality rules before the firm spun off from KPMG.

During his tenure, Wright worked on high-profile insolvencies and restructurings, including Claire’s Accessories, TGI Fridays, and Heart With Smart Restaurants. 

The group appointed long-standing managing directors Russell Downs and Rick Harrison to co-lead the UK restructuring practice following Wright’s resignation.

Beyond restructuring

Its restructuring practice is still the largest part of its business. In its 2025 results, the last time Interpath disclosed a revenue split, advisory, which covers deal advisory, value creation, and forensics, surged 82 per cent to £76.1m. Restructuring still accounted for the majority of the business at £122.8m, but it grew more slowly. 

Fiona Czerniawska, CEO of Source Global Research, told City AM that the restructuring market has fewer large projects. 

“The restructuring market used to be enormous and very cyclical,” she said. “[We] had some very big restructuring projects, and still do, but there are a smaller number of them, and more is being done to try and avert that happening.” 

As a professional services firm, Interpath’s people are its business, especially those deemed ‘rainmakers’.

In Interpath’s 2025 UK accounts going concern note, the advisory firm highlighted that people are the company’s ‘key asset’ and that retaining high-quality people is critical to “continued growth and success is critical”. 

“If the company lost the services of either a number of revenue-generating managing directors, or a large number of delivery employees, this could result in an adverse effect on the company, its business operations and financial condition,” the note said. 

Despite the six recent losses, the group has also added 40 managing directors to the leadership team over the past year, including lateral hires from EY, Kroll in the UK, Alvarez & Marsal in Germany and Grant Thornton in India.

When approached for comment, an Interpath spokesperson said: “Interpath continues to go from strength to strength, delivering £250m in revenue in FY26, with strong earnings momentum continuing this year.”

“Today, we have more than 1,200 people, including over 150 managing directors across 36 locations, and expect to have appointed 40 new managing directors by year-end. With Bridgepoint’s continued firepower, we remain focused on investing in our people and expanding internationally,” they added.

In the same week a report warned that Britain was on the verge of losing an entire generation to worklessness, the Labour government signed a new youth mobility deal with the EU.

Under the new scheme, the UK would offer 100,000 visas a year to EU citizens, with this being reciprocated. But if Andy Burnham was so serious about achieving what report author Alan Milburn has called ‘NEET Zero’ – the goal of having every single young Briton in some form of education, employment or training – would he have signed up to such a migration partnership with the EU?

First, it should be noted that this new UK-EU youth mobility scheme is different to freedom of movement – there is an annual cap, restrictions in terms of age, and a time limit of up to three years (initially two years with a one-year extension option) on the visas. However, the allocation of 100,000 visas a year comfortably exceeds the limit of 30,000 people wanted by Burnham’s predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer. Also, there are serious concerns over the timing of the Labour government signing this migration pact with the EU, considering that the UK has nearly 1m young NEETs. According to the most recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures, 981,000 people aged 16-24 years are not in education, employment, and training – 13 per cent of this age group, rising to 13.7 per cent for males. There is a crisis of youth inactivity in modern Britain.

By signing up to the youth mobility pact with the EU, the UK government is essentially inviting hundreds of thousands of young Europeans to come to Britain – increasing competition for jobs in sectors such as hospitality and retail, as well as entry-level roles. Poorer EU member-states with high levels of youth unemployment and existing diaspora networks in the UK – such as Romania – are likely to be prominent countries of origin among young European people who will benefit from this new visa scheme. Increasing the supply of foreign workers willing to take lower-paid and casual roles will reduce pressure on employers to raise pay and improve working conditions for domestic candidates.

Low wages and poor conditions

While the UK-EU youth mobility pact may please some bosses in Britain who are happy to keep wages low and offer substandard working conditions, it is not in the interests of the country of large – especially younger Britons in need of opportunities. And if they do entertain the possibility of moving abroad, they are more likely to look at Anglosphere and Commonwealth nations such as Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, along with the United States.

The UK-EU youth mobility arrangement will be characterised by asymmetrical take-up. Based on historical trends and widespread English proficiency, it is highly likely that far more EU citizens will come to the UK than the other way around – contributing towards higher net migration.

As a result of his Euro-obsession, Burnham risks betraying the localist values of his beloved ‘Manchesterism’ as well as neglecting the strong cultural ties the UK has with the English-speaking democracies of the Anglosphere. Roughly 3.5m people will receive their annual tax code notices electronically from February 2027, as part of the tax authority’s plans to reduce spending on paper correspondence and postage and become a digital-first office.

The body’s annual print, postage and office supplies bill exceeded £70m in the 2025/26 financial year, according to its most recent accounts.

The change applies to people already using HMRC’s Personal Tax Account or app but yet to make the transition to online notices. Around 20m taxpayers currently use this service.

Customers who do not yet use the office’s online services will continue to receive their tax code notice through the post.

Encouraging digitalisation

The move comes as HMRC shifts more information online in its bid to encourage more customers to go paperless. It has committed to saving more than £50m a year in print and post costs from the 2028/29 financial year.

The body confirmed that of the 17.5m tax codes for the 2026/27 issued ahead of 6 April 2026, 34 per cent were digital, but 11.5m were posted at a cost of more than £8.2m.

James Murray, Financial Secretary to the Treasury and Paymaster General, said: “This will modernise the service it provides and will reduce the amount of taxpayers’ money being spent on printing and postage.

“Making annual tax code notices digital by default…is the first step to reduce print and postal costs.”

Monitoring changes

Industry figures noted that moving codes online is a “logical next step” for people using the app, but warned that a failure to properly inform some taxpayers of the change may lead to more issues.

“Convenience will count for little if taxpayers miss the message,” said Joseph Adunse, tax partner at Moore Kingston Smith.

“HMRC should monitor whether people are reading notices rather than simply ignoring the alerts. Those affected first are likely to be digitally savvy, but even they face a relentless stream of app notifications and emails. Important tax notices can easily disappear into digital noise.”

HMRC said it will monitor how the affected taxpayers respond to the new approach, including whether they ultimately view their code online, contact HMRC or request a paper copy in order to inform the wider digital rollout.

On this day, 25 November 2016, Cuban revolutionary Fidel Castro passed away aged 90 years old. Castro became, and remains, the murderous dictator it’s acceptable for mainstream politicians to admire, writes Eliot Wilson

Ten years ago today, Cubavisión, the state broadcaster of the Republic of Cuba, scrambled to broadcast an unexpected address by the President of the Council of State and First Secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba, 85-year old Raúl Castro.

“With deep pain, I appear to inform our people and our friends across America and the world that today, 25 November 2016, at 10:29 p.m., the Commander-in-Chief of the Cuban Revolution, Fidel Castro Ruz, passed away… In compliance with the expressed will of Comrade Fidel, his remains will be cremated in the early hours of Saturday 26; the funeral organising committee will provide our people with detailed information on the organisation of the posthumous tribute to the founder of the Cuban Revolution. ¡Hasta la victoria siempre!”

That last phrase, “Ever onward to victory!”, had been the sign-off of Che Guevara’s letter to Fidel Castro in 1965; the Argentinian revolutionary, iconic on a million posters and T-shirts, had resigned as Minister of Industries and was leaving to spread the gospel of Marxist-Leninist revolution in Africa and South America. Two and a half years later, Guevara was dead, clumsily executed by a half-drunk sergeant from the Bolivian Rangers. But Castro still had a long way to go.

The birth of Fidel Castro

Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz was born a century ago, the son of a wealthy farmer and self-made businessman, originally from Galicia, and his mistress and housemaid, with whom he had six other children. Castro was educated at Jesuit-run schools on Santiago de Cuba, then in 1945 he enrolled at the University of Havana to read law. Inevitably, as the son of a hard-bitten entrepreneur, he was soon immersed in radical left-wing, anti-American and anti-imperialist student politics.

That Spain, the land of his father’s birth, had been the imperial power in Cuba for nearly 400 years did not faze him. Nor was he held back by any irony in joining the Party of the Cuban People – Orthodox, the slogan of which was Vergüenza contra dinero, “Shame against money”. For the young, revolution is always a cleansing fire.

Castro never lacked ambition. Before he was 21, he was volunteering for a military operation to unseat the President and Generalissimo of the Dominican Republic, Rafael Trujillo; in 1948 he went to Bogotá, to protest at the foundation of the Organization of American States, just weeks after the assassination of the Leader of the Colombian Liberal Party, Jorge Eliécer Gaitán.

Already well known as a left-wing activist, Castro still somehow managed to graduate as a doctor of law and start a legal practice, but his intense focus was politics, and the politics of revolution. When Major General Fulgencio Batista installed himself as President in 1954, practising what he called “disciplined democracy” and fuelled by deals with US sugar and fruit exporters and the Mob, Castro was given his purpose: to oust Batista and “free” the people of Cuba, even if he had to forge a dictatorship to do it.

First impressions on the world stage

A mood was shifting. If the United States had played a many-layered game during the Second World War partly to undermine the British Empire – and it had, successfully – the heady breezes of decolonisation, both physical and economic, were gusting through the Caribbean too. This was America’s back yard, the Monroe Doctrine had said so since 1823; but the people of Cuba, like those of the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, Panama, Colombia, Nicaragua or Guatemala, would not in perpetuity accept the substitution of the power of the dollar for the imperial occupation by Spain.

Having spent most of the 1950s waging the Cuban Revolution, Castro arrived in Havana on 9 January 1959 in triumph. Batista had fled the previous month and Castro had wrong-footed his rival against the régime, General Eulogio Cantillo. He had won hearts and minds: the liberal lawyer Manuel Urrutia Lleó was installed as a figurehead President, but it was Castro, initially as Representative of the Rebel Armed Forces of the Presidency, who was making the decisions. A month later, he became Prime Minister, a position he would hold for 17 years before transitioning to President of the Council of State, stepping down only in 2008, into his 80s.

At first it was hard to know what to make of Castro. His image was perfect: tall and imposing, in army fatigues, with a resplendent beard and long cigar, he had charisma to spare and was a gifted orator, though as his rule went on his speeches became endurance tests. In 1960, he harangued the UN General Assembly for four-and-a-half-hours, but his record was probably 1998, when he addressed the Cuban National Assembly for seven hours and 15 minutes.

Castro did not immediately style himself as a Communist, even if the United States still had a cohort who thought that anyone to the left of Adlai Stevenson was a suspected Red. After hosting Castro in Washington in April 1959, Vice President Richard Nixon told the press cautiously, “He is either incredibly naive about Communism or under Communist discipline – my guess is the former”. But 1962 changed everything, made everything startlingly clear.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 is often regarded as the closest the Cold War came to running hot. One clumsy move by either side could have brought the tension to a boil. Although Nikita Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the thermonuclear medium-range ballistic missiles from Cuba, which would have cut any warning the United States might have had from hours to minutes or effectively none at all, it showed that Cuba was a dagger at the throat of America and Castro was willing to brandish it. Relations between the two countries went into deep-freeze and have yet to thaw.

Castro’s death and legacy

By the time he died, it was almost impossible to comprehend how long Castro had spent on the world stage. He had been a thorn in the side of the Eisenhower administration; Harold Macmillan was Prime Minister; and the French Fourth Republic was still in its death throes. He was backed by Khrushchev and the Soviet Union. By 2016, there were carefully worded neutral formulations from Barack Obama and Theresa May, and warm tributes from President Francois Hollande and Vladimir Putin.

President-elect Donald Trump hid nothing: “Today, the world marks the passing of a brutal dictator who oppressed his own people for nearly six decades.” His reaction on Twitter had been more concise: “Fidel Castro is dead!”

Most baffling to many is how Castro became, and remains, the murderous dictator it’s acceptable for mainstream politicians to admire and praise. Certainly the United States had been clumsy, aggressive and paranoid in its approach to Cuba. But Castro was a brutal autocrat: 4,000 executions and extrajudicial killings may seem an underachievement in today’s world, but tens of thousands were held as political prisoners in a one-party state, and in the mid-1960s something like one in 400 of the population was incarcerated for political reasons.

And Cuba is a country beggared. Nine-tenths of Cubans live in extreme poverty, pharmaceuticals are frequently absent, rationing of food has been imposed several times, the population is ageing and falling. The Covid-19 pandemic slammed into Cuba violently, slashing the vital tourism sector. Yet Fidel Castro, a dictator for nearly 50 years, is an icon to many.

Sometimes nations have to choose between freedom and prosperity. Sometimes both can be achieved. It is the tragedy of the Cuban people that they have neither. ¡Viva Cuba libre! And soon.

Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink
