The post Somali Airlines targets 10 December relaunch after a 35-year hiatus appeared first on AGN.

]]> After several delayed relaunch plans, Somalia has set a new date to revive its national carrier as the government advances efforts to rebuild the country’s aviation sector.

Somali Airlines is set to resume operations on 10 December, more than three decades after the national carrier ceased flying, Somalia’s Transport and Civil Aviation Ministers Mohamed Farah Nuh told reporters on Monday.

Nuh said that preparations were underway, with an official launch ceremony planned for next month to celebrate the state-owned airline’s return.

“Somali Airlines is returning this coming December, and its official launch will take place then,” he said, according to Somali news outlet Hiraan.

🚨| BREAKING NEWS: Somalia’s Minister of Transport and Civil #Aviation, Mohamed Farah Nuh, has officially announced that the nation’s historic flag carrier, #Somali #Airlines, will make its long-awaited return to the skies on December 10, this year. Speaking on the milestone revival, Minister Nuh assured the public that the return of the national airline is imminent. Somali #Airlines is being brought back this coming December, and its official launch will be seen," Minister Nuh said, confirming that citizens will certainly witness the historic comeback next month during the December 10 inauguration ceremony. Under international aviation rules, sending out the code confirms that Somali Airlines is legally certified to operate across borders. This global notification ensures that radar systems, airports, and airspace controllers in every country around the world officially recognize and accept Somali Airlines flights as the carrier prepares to resume international operations after more than three decades. #SomaliAirlines #Aviation #ICAO #Mogadishu #BreakingNews

— Abdikarin Dahir (@Abdikarindahirr) November 23, 2026

Somali Airlines has failed to meet previous relaunch dates

The announcement follows postponed relaunch deadlines. In August, the airline said it planned to resume operations in September, but that deadline passed without a return to commercial operations.

The airline, which was established in 1964, ceased operations in 1991 after the overthrow of President Siad Barre and the collapse of the country’s central government.

The latest relaunch plans follow the government’s acquisition of two Airbus A320s as part of its planned return to service earlier this year. Hiiraan also reported that the airline has arranged to lease a Dash 8-400 turboprop aircraft from regional operator, Daallo Airlines.

However, neither the government nor the airlines have publicly confirmed details of the leasing agreement. Similarly, while the two Airbus aircraft Somalia has acquired have been identified as A320-200s, their registrations and who they are being purchased from have also yet to be disclosed.

Prior to its collapse, Somali Airlines operated domestic and international flights from its hub in Mogadishu connecting Somalia with destinations across Africa, the Middle East and Europe.

International airlines currently serving Somalia

Mogadishu’s Aden Adde International Airport is served by several international carriers, including Ethiopian Airlines, Uganda Airlines, SalamAir, Qatar Airways, Etihad Airways, Egypt Air, ITA Airways and Turkish Airlines.

Regional and Somali-linked operators also serve the landlocked country. These include Air Djibouti, based at Djibouti-Ambouli International Airport; Jubba Airways, a Somali-origin carrier headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya, with a presence in Mogadishu; and Daallo Airlines.

Rebuilding Somalia’s aviation infrastructure

The planned relaunch of Somali Airlines coincides with Somalia’s wider efforts to rebuild its aviation infrastructure, including plans for a new airport at Mahay, intended to eventually replace Mogadishu’s existing international airport.

Construction preparations for the greenfield airport began in June 2025, with the project estimated to cost between US$800 million and US$1 billion. Completion is targeted for the end of the decade.

Somalia’s Civil Aviation Authority (SCAA) has described the new airport as a “bold visionary leap”, saying it would transform the country’s air transport network, strengthen connectivity, “ignite economic momentum and open gateways for our youth.”

The long-awaited return of Somali Airlines, alongside investment in airport infrastructure, forms part of Somalia’s broader ambition to reconnect with regional and international aviation markets.

Whether the 10 December deadline is met will depend on completing preparations, aircraft availability, and necessary regulatory approvals.

]]> ESA’s Hera reaches asteroid struck by NASA in historic planetary defence test https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/esa-hera-reaches-dimorphos-dart-impact-damage/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:06:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57913 More than four years after NASA’s DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos, ESA’s Hera has arrived to inspect the damage and measure the asteroid’s mass.

The post ESA’s Hera reaches asteroid struck by NASA in historic planetary defence test appeared first on AGN.

]]> More than four years after NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid to change its course, the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has has arrived at the Didymos asteroid system to investigate the full extent of the damage caused by the collision.

ESA will unveil Hera’s first close-up images of the asteroid Dimorphos later today (25 November), following the spacecraft’s two-year journey through deep space.

The mission will establish how much the asteroid was physically altered by the impact, measure its mass and examine its internal structure. And the findings could help scientists determine how to deflect an asteroid should one ever be discovered on a collision course with Earth.

NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) demonstrated in September 2022 that a spacecraft could deliberately change the motion of a celestial body. Subsequent research revealed that the collision had also altered the asteroid’s shape and even changed its path around the Sun.

Neither Dimorphos nor its larger companion, Didymos, poses a threat to Earth.

Hera’s first images of Dimorphos will be presented at Berlin’s Museum für Naturkunde, with a live broadcast beginning at 19:45 CET (18:45 GMT).

ESA has chosen the museum’s dinosaur hall as the venue for the event. Some 66 million years ago, an asteroid impact caused a mass extinction that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.

“‘We’re here to put a dent in the Universe,’ is what Steve Jobs famously declared,” said Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli.

“Through many years of hard work our international collaboration managed to do just that, and for the very highest of intentions: to help make Earth safer.”

Carnelli said the event would also recognise the work of the mission team, which overcame initial difficulties securing funding, the COVID-19 pandemic and an approaching hurricane shortly before launch.

What happened when NASA crashed DART into an asteroid?

Launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in November 2021, DART was the first space mission specifically designed to test whether an asteroid could be deflected by deliberately striking it with a spacecraft.

The target was Dimorphos, a roughly 151-metre-wide asteroid orbiting the much larger, 730-metre-wide Didymos. The two objects form what astronomers call a binary asteroid system.

On 26 September 2022, the approximately half-tonne DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos at 6.1 kilometres per second, or nearly 22,000 kilometres per hour.

The collision was observed by the Italian Space Agency’s LICIACube satellite, the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes and ground-based observatories.

It sent millions of kilograms of rocky material into space, creating a trail of debris extending more than 10,000 kilometres. The debris remained visible for months.

Before the collision, Dimorphos took approximately 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit Didymos. The impact shortened that period by around 33 minutes, substantially exceeding NASA’s minimum expectations.

However, scientists subsequently discovered that the collision had done far more than change the asteroid’s orbit.

DART changed the shape of Dimorphos

A study led by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), published in March 2024, found that Dimorphos had undergone a significant change in shape.

Before the impact, the asteroid resembled a flattened ball and followed a circular orbit around Didymos. Computer models developed using spacecraft imagery, radar measurements and telescope observations indicated that it had become more elongated.

“When DART made impact, things got very interesting,” said Shantanu Naidu, a navigation engineer at JPL who led the study.

The researchers calculated that the orbital period had shortened by 33 minutes and 15 seconds, settling at 11 hours, 22 minutes and three seconds.

Dimorphos was also orbiting approximately 37 metres closer to Didymos than before the collision.

The findings supported the theory that Dimorphos is a rubble-pile asteroid, essentially a collection of rocks and dust held together by weak gravitational forces rather than a single solid mass.

Hera will now allow scientists to examine those changes directly and establish whether DART left a distinct impact crater or reshaped the entire asteroid.

How flying debris helped move an asteroid

In August 2025, NASA published further research based on images captured by LICIACube, which had separated from DART 15 days before the collision.

The small Italian spacecraft photographed the impact debris from several angles, capturing its closest image from just 85.3 kilometres above the asteroid’s surface.

Researchers estimated that the collision had dislodged around 16 million kilograms of dust and rock. Although this represented less than 0.5% of Dimorphos’s total mass, it was approximately 30,000 times the mass of DART itself.

The material thrown into space provided an additional push, making the deflection more effective than the spacecraft’s impact alone.

“The plume of material released from the asteroid was like a short burst from a rocket engine,” said Ramin Lolachi, a research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center who led the study.

Dave Glenar, a planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, who participated in the research, said many near-Earth asteroids were expected to have a structure similar to Dimorphos.

“So, this extra push from the debris plume is critical to consider when building future spacecraft to deflect asteroids from Earth.”

Understanding how different types of asteroids respond to an impact will be important when designing future planetary defence missions.

NASA also changed an asteroid’s orbit around the Sun

Another discovery, announced by NASA in March 2026, revealed that DART had altered the path of the entire Didymos-Dimorphos system around the Sun.

Research published in the journal Science Advances found that the collision had changed the binary asteroid system’s 770-day solar orbital period by 0.15 seconds.

It was the first measurable alteration of a celestial body’s path around the Sun caused by a human-made object.

Researchers used radar measurements and observations from volunteer astronomers who recorded 22 occasions between October 2022 and March 2025 when the asteroid passed in front of distant stars.

“This is a tiny change to the orbit, but given enough time, even a tiny change can grow to a significant deflection,” said Thomas Statler, lead scientist for solar system small bodies at NASA Headquarters.

The discovery is particularly relevant to planetary defence. An asteroid detected sufficiently early could potentially be diverted away from Earth through a relatively small change in its velocity.

What will ESA’s Hera spacecraft investigate?

Hera, Europe’s first planetary defence mission, was launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on 7 October 2024.

The spacecraft flew past Mars on 12 March 2025, using the planet’s gravity to adjust its trajectory while also photographing its smaller moon, Deimos.

A further manoeuvre in February 2026 placed Hera on course for Didymos. Braking manoeuvres in October reduced its speed relative to the asteroids ahead of its rendezvous.

At the time of arrival, the asteroid system was approximately 195 million kilometres from Earth.

Built by a European industrial consortium led by Germany’s OHB, Hera weighs approximately 1,081 kilograms when fully fuelled. Its solar panels span 11.5 metres when deployed.

Together with its two smaller companion spacecraft, Hera carries 11 scientific instruments and a radio science experiment.

One of the mission’s most important objectives is to establish the precise mass of Dimorphos. Without that information, scientists cannot accurately determine how efficiently DART transferred momentum to the asteroid.

Hera will also investigate the asteroid’s internal structure, surface composition and altered orbit.

“How did the impact change Dimorphos? What is the mass of the asteroid and which of its properties explain its response to DART impact?” said Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS and the Observatoire de la Cote d’Azur.

During the initial six-week survey, Hera will fly at distances of between 20 and 30 kilometres from the asteroids. Subsequent operations will bring the spacecraft within eight to 10 kilometres, allowing scientists to map their surfaces in greater detail.

Later phases will include 12 close flybys covering much of Dimorphos’s surface, including the DART impact site.

Two miniature spacecraft will investigate Dimorphos

Hera is also carrying two shoebox-sized satellites, Juventas and Milani, which are scheduled to be deployed in early 2027.

Juventas carries a low-frequency radar designed to examine the asteroid’s interior. The measurements could establish how rocks and other material are distributed beneath its surface.

Towards the end of its mission, Juventas will attempt to land on Dimorphos and use a miniature gravimeter to measure the asteroid’s extremely weak gravitational field.

Milani will examine the surface composition of both asteroids and study dust in their surroundings. It may also attempt a landing at the end of its mission.

The two CubeSats will communicate with Hera through inter-satellite radio links, allowing the main spacecraft to relay their scientific data to Earth.

The 25 Nov unveiling is only the start of Hera’s exploration, ESA’s Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers said ahead of Wednesday’s event.

“In the next few months we will be flying closer to the asteroids, and early in the new year will deploy a pair of shoebox-sized CubeSats to take extra risks and venture even nearer than the main spacecraft,” Kueppers said.

Could humanity prevent a future asteroid impact?

Although major asteroid impacts are rare, relatively small objects can cause considerable damage.

The 2013 Chelyabinsk event in Russia involved an asteroid measuring approximately 20 metres across. Its explosion in the atmosphere generated a shockwave that struck six cities.

ESA’s Near-Earth Object Coordination Centre in Italy works alongside NASA’s Center for Near-Earth Object Studies to identify potentially hazardous asteroids, calculate their trajectories and assess the risks they pose.

NASA is also developing its Near-Earth Object Surveyor space telescope to detect asteroids and comets that are difficult to identify using visible-light observations.

Early detection remains central to any attempt to divert a hazardous asteroid. The more time scientists have before a predicted collision, the smaller the change in its trajectory may need to be.

DART demonstrated that humans could deliberately alter an asteroid’s motion. Hera’s task over the coming months is to establish precisely how that happened and whether the results can be reproduced when Earth’s safety depends on it.

]]> Could Ukraine fly America’s retired F-15 Eagles? A former US general makes the case https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/us-retired-f15-eagles-ukraine-transfer/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 13:35:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57886 Why it arguably makes sense for Washington to transfer dozens of retired F-15 Eagles to Ukraine and why it is highly unlikely to.

The post Could Ukraine fly America’s retired F-15 Eagles? A former US general makes the case appeared first on AGN.

]]> Retired United States Air Force Lieutenant General David A. Deptula has written an opinion piece for Forbes arguing that the US should consider transferring 50-60 retired F-15C/Ds to Ukraine.

Deptula is now the dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies think tank. He is also a senior scholar at the U.S. Air Force Academy’s Institute for Future Conflict. The retired general recently returned from Ukraine, where he worked with the Ukrainian Air Force to improve its air operations.

The US has hundreds of mothballed retired F-15C/Ds

Deptula argues that Ukraine is in sore need of more fighter jets and that the US’s recently retired F-15C/Ds stored at the Davis-Monthan boneyard could be a solution. These have been replaced by F-35As and F-15EXs in US Air Force service.

He writes, “The United States should assess whether it can refurbish, equip, and transfer roughly 50–60 F-15C/D Eagles to Ukraine.”

The US has over 240 F-15C/Ds in storage at the Arizona boneyard, with more expected to join in the next few years. Some of these would require little work to be ready to be transferred.

Ukraine needs more aircraft in the air at any one point in time than it can manage with its existing fleet; fighter jets are indispensable for fighting off Russian air attacks.

Ukraine’s F-16s, Mirage 2000s, and legacy Soviet era fighters pay for these missions in heavy maintenance. He argues that with its fighters tied up in air defence, Ukraine lacks units to carry out offensive missions against Russia.

A case for sending F-15C/Ds to Ukraine

The F-15 Eagle is a much larger aircraft than the light/medium weight F-16 and can carry more rounds (940 vs 511 rounds) and many more rockets for short-range air defence. If older F-15s could take over air defence, then Ukraine’s F-16s could receive multirole missions for which they are better suited.

Some of the retired F-15C/Ds have received the APG-63(V)3 active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, giving pilots markedly better detection range, tracking, and reliability than the radars on the F-16s or any of Ukraine’s other fighters.

He says the strongest argument is speed, as it takes time to produce and deliver new F-16s, Gripens, and Rafales. It also takes over a year to train pilots and maintenance crews.

Deptula notes, “Introducing another fighter type will pose some challenges for Ukraine: pilot training, maintenance, spare parts, ground equipment, infrastructure, and weapons supply must be resolved before aircraft are transferred.”

Washington unlikely to transfer F-15C/Ds to Ukraine

Even under the Biden administration, Washington refused to transfer retired F-16 Fighting Falcons to Ukraine, even though it has hundreds sitting mothballed in its boneyard.

This is not to say Washington didn’t aid Ukraine with F-16s. It did and does. Washington provided critical training and other facilitation roles, but it insisted the airframes had to come from European stocks.

In the last few weeks of 2026, Ukraine is expected to receive ten ex-Belgium F-16s, two ex-French Mirage 2000-5F, and possibly two or so ex-Polish MiG-29s depending on that particular set of colourful negotiations. The first of 16 ex-Swedish Gripen C/Ds are to arrive in January 2027.

🇺🇦 Ukraine will begin receiving Swedish Gripen aircraft in January 2027, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on November 23 📸: Wikipedia 🔗https://t.co/QjBBLbvX8m https://t.co/5fT4TrDcLW

— The New Voice of Ukraine (@NewVoiceUkraine) November 24, 2026

There is some wisdom to the maxim “never say never”, but under the current Trump administration, it seems highly unlikely it would seriously consider transferring old Eagles to Ukraine.

The latest opinion piece is no revelation that Uncle Sam has deep stores of active and mothballed fighter jets that Europe collectively lacks. The latest piece is an opinion of what Washington could do if it chose to, not a realistic assessment of what it will likely choose to do.

Instead, Ukraine is looking long-term to Europeans for its fighter needs. Its ageing, worn-out, and attrited fleet of Soviet Su-25s, Su-24s, MiG-29s, and Su-27s is likely to retire at the earliest convenience post-war.

These will be replaced by a fleet of up to 250 fighters (subject to political, financial, and industrial constraints). The fleet is to be made up primarily of Saab Gripens (mostly new Es), Rafales, and older ex-European F-16s.

]]> EASA adds eight Airbus A380s to accelerated wing crack checks https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/easa-airbus-a380-wing-crack-inspections-eight-more/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:58:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57901 EASA has added eight Airbus A380s to the group requiring accelerated inspections for cracks in the wing mid spars, with an inspection deadline of 31 January 2027.

The post EASA adds eight Airbus A380s to accelerated wing crack checks appeared first on AGN.

]]> Eight more Airbus A380s will require wing crack inspections before 31 January 2027. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) added the aircraft to an earlier list of superjumbos that need checks after Airbus found a potential problem with the wing mid-spars, structural members that help carry the wing’s loads. EASA says cracking in this part of the wing could weaken the structure if it goes undetected and uncorrected.

The new airworthiness directive took effect on 18 November. It replaces the emergency order EASA issued in June, when a check on one A380 turned up what the agency called “an unexpected level of findings”.

Further analysis brought the list from 16 aircraft to 24. Emirates operates 22 of the affected aircraft. Etihad Airways and Qantas operate one each, according to Aviation Week’s fleet data.

What the inspections are looking for

EASA’s December 2025 directive identified areas to check on both wings, including parts of the mid rear spar and the inner and outer mid front spars. A review of those inspection results led to the emergency order in June.

Aviation Week reported that hydrogen embrittlement had accelerated cracking in some wing spars on A380s that spent extended periods in storage. The process makes metal less able to deform under stress, so cracks can develop more readily.

When the 24 Airbus A380s need to be checked

The eight aircraft added in November have a January deadline. For the 16 already on the list, the original deadlines still apply. As AGN reported in June, five needed an inspection before their first flight after 24 June, with a limited allowance to fly without passengers to a maintenance site. The other 11 were permitted up to 25 take-offs and landings from that date.

Qantas told AGN in June that its affected A380, VH-OQI, was already in Dresden, Germany, for heavy maintenance. The airline said at the time that the emergency order would not affect its flight schedule.

Operators can count inspections they already carried out under the relevant Airbus instructions. The eight newly listed aircraft are subject to Airbus’s inspection instructions dated 6 November.

Aircraft coming out of storage need a check before flying

The November directive also changes what airlines must do when they bring an A380 back from long-term storage. An A380-841, A380-842 or A380-861 that has spent more than 12 months in storage needs a wing mid-spar inspection before it returns to service. The rule applies after each qualifying storage period.

Once an aircraft returns to service following a check under the directive, the operator has up to 36 months to inspect it again. The next check must also take place within 42 months of the start of the previous inspection. Whichever deadline comes first applies.

If inspectors find a problem, the airline must contact Airbus before the next flight and follow the manufacturer’s repair timetable. Airbus also asks for the results of checks that find nothing. Operators have 30 days to report, counted from the inspection date.

EASA says the November directive is an interim measure and further requirements may follow. The agency issued the directive ahead of consultation and asked for comments before 9 December.

]]> Malaysia Airlines picks Boeing 787-10 to replace its Airbus A350s https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/malaysia-airlines-boeing-787-10-airbus-a350-replacement/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:12:34 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57911 Malaysia Aviation Group has committed to 10 Boeing 787-10 Dreamliners, with options for six more. Malaysia Airlines would become the first Malaysian Dreamliner operator.

The post Malaysia Airlines picks Boeing 787-10 to replace its Airbus A350s appeared first on AGN.

]]> Malaysia Aviation Group (MAG) has committed to buying 10 Boeing 787-10 Dreamliners, with options for six more. The new Dreamliners would replace Malaysia Airlines’ seven Airbus A350s. 

The purchase would make Malaysia Airlines the country’s first Dreamliner operator. The group expects deliveries from 2032 to 2035. 

Malaysia’s new 787-10s are “a strategic investment in the future” 

MAG announced the acquisition at a signing ceremony in Kuala Lumpur on 25 November, attended by Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

“The acquisition of the 787 Dreamliner represents a strategic investment in the future of Malaysia Aviation Group,” said Captain Nasaruddin A. Bakar, President and Group Chief Executive Officer of MAG, in the company’s announcement.  “As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility, while delivering the elevated travel experience our customers expect. Beyond fleet renewal, this investment reinforces our commitment to maintaining a modern, competitive airline that supports Malaysia’s connectivity and global aspirations.”

Boeing said Malaysia Airlines intends to make the 787-10 its next flagship.

Erika Pearson, Boeing vice president of Sales and Marketing for Southeast Asia and Oceania, said: “Malaysia Aviation Group is shaping its future long-haul fleet with the 787 Dreamliner’s unmatched efficiency and signature passenger experience. We’re delighted to build on our long-standing partnership and strengthen connections with Malaysia as the 787-10 plays an integral role in the airline’s next chapter.”

The 787-10 is the largest member of the Dreamliner family, and MAG plans to fit 319 seats across three classes on the aircraft, but did not disclose how it plans to distribute seats among the three cabin classes.

The group will phase out its seven A350S over the four-year period until the new Dreamliners arrive.

Where Malaysia Airlines plans to fly the 787-10

The airline plans to use the extra seats available on the 787-10 on selected, high-demand long-haul routes. MAG named London, Paris, Sydney, Melbourne, Tokyo, Osaka and Seoul as markets the new aircraft could serve. 

The initial commitment for 10 aircraft would give the airline three more jets than it has in its current A350 fleet, increasing its overall capacity. Taking up all six options would grow the airline’s long-haul fleet by nine aircraft compared to today. 

Boeing returns to the airline’s widebody fleet

Malaysia Airlines previously flew Boeing 747s and 777s. The Dreamliner would bring Boeing back into a widebody fleet that has been renewing with Airbus aircraft. 

In 2022, the airline committed to acquiring 20 A330neos. The airline received its first A330neo in November 2024 through lessor Avolon. Airbus announced a firm order for another 20 A330-900s in July 2025, taking the planned A330neo fleet to 40. 

The A330neo programme was already underway when MAG set out its plans to replace the A350s with Dreamliners over the next decade.

The carrier’s Boeing fleet today consists of narrowbody 737s. Boeing lists 19 737-8s and 38 previous-generation 737s in service with Malaysia Airlines, alongside 18 737-8s and 12 737-10s on order. MAG says the remaining aircraft under its wider 737 programme, which includes leased jets, are due by 2030. 

Malaysia confirms GEnx-1B engines for new 787-10s

The Dreamliner agreement also extends the airline’s relationship with GE Aerospace. MAG also announced it would power the 787-10 with GE Aerospace GEnx-1B engines. MAG also renewed its agreements for GE’s Fuel Insight and FlightPulse software, which the group uses to assess fuel use and support operational decisions.

Jason Tonich, Chief Commercial Sales & Customer Officer of GE Aerospace, said, “We are honoured to begin this new chapter in our nearly three-decade relationship with MAG. The GEnx has established itself as one of the most proven and successful widebody engines of its generation, delivering the reliability, durability, and fuel efficiency our customers need to operate across some of the world’s most demanding routes.”

Boeing has a composites operation in Malaysia which supplies parts and subassemblies for its commercial aircraft programmes, including the 787. The plant is Boeing’s first wholly owned manufacturing facility in Southeast Asia.

]]> Boeing wins order for 15 more KC-46 tankers amid debate over USAF refuelling strategy https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/boeing-us-air-force-contract-15-kc-46a-pegasus-tankers/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 09:47:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57891 Boeing has won a US Air Force contract for 15 more KC-46A Pegasus tankers, bringing total orders to 203 and extending 767 production beyond 2027.

The post Boeing wins order for 15 more KC-46 tankers amid debate over USAF refuelling strategy appeared first on AGN.

]]> Boeing has secured a contract from the US Air Force (USAF) to build 15 additional KC-46A Pegasus tankers, just weeks after an independent study urged the service to reconsider further purchases of the aircraft in favour of a new generation of longer-range tankers.

The latest order brings the total number of KC-46As contracted by the US Air Force and international customers to 203.

The contract also comes at an important time for Boeing’s 767 programme. Commercial production of the widebody is scheduled to end in 2027, but military orders for the KC-46A, which is derived from the 767, will keep the production line running for years to come.

“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” said Jake Kwasnik, Boeing’s KC-46 programme vice president.

“The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”

Boeing has so far delivered 116 KC-46As to the US Air Force, six to the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and two to the Israeli Air Force.

The airframer said the US Air Force’s KC-46A fleet had accumulated more than 180,000 flight hours since the first aircraft was delivered in 2019.

US Air Force urged to reconsider KC-46 purchases

As reported previously by Aerospace Global News, a study by the Washington-based Hudson Institute questioned whether continued investment in the KC-46A would adequately meet the US military’s future aerial refuelling requirements.

The report, Resilient Reach: Redesigning Aerial Refueling for Contested Global Operations, was written by researchers Timothy A. Walton and Shane Dennin.

While acknowledging the Pegasus’s performance in current operations, the researchers argued that its range, fuel delivery capacity and survivability could limit its effectiveness in future conflicts, particularly across the Indo-Pacific.

“The medium-range KC-46A has performed well in contemporary operations and would play an important role in any conflict,” the researchers said.

However, their modelling suggested that a medium-sized blended-wing-body (BWB) tanker could refuel more than twice as many groups of combat aircraft as the KC-46A or support them at more than twice the distance.

Unlike conventional aircraft, a blended-wing design merges the fuselage and wings into a continuous lifting surface, reducing aerodynamic drag and potentially improving fuel efficiency. The further a tanker travels to reach other aircraft, the more fuel it consumes itself, leaving less available to transfer.

The study estimated that acquiring and operating 250 blended-wing-body tankers could save $15.5 billion over 30 years compared with an equivalent fleet of KC-46As. Those figures are based on computer modelling rather than the demonstrated performance of an operational tanker.

The US Air Force is already exploring the technology. In 2023, it awarded California-based JetZero a contract to develop a full-scale blended-wing-body demonstrator in partnership with Northrop Grumman.

The demonstrator is scheduled to fly by the end of 2027, although an operational tanker based on such a configuration remains some way off.

KC-46 Pegasus: A programme beset by challenges

The latest order adds to a tanker programme that has experienced procurement controversies, development delays, technical difficulties and substantial financial losses for Boeing.

The US Air Force selected Boeing’s 767-based tanker in 2011 following a lengthy competition involving a rival proposal based on the Airbus A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT).

The original programme envisaged the acquisition of 179 aircraft to begin replacing the ageing KC-135 Stratotanker fleet, which entered service in 1957.

Adapting an established commercial aircraft was expected to reduce development risks. However, integrating the military systems proved more complicated than anticipated.

Among the most persistent problems has been the KC-46A’s Remote Vision System (RVS), which allows boom operators to conduct aerial refuelling using cameras and digital displays rather than looking directly through a window at the receiving aircraft.

Problems with image quality under certain lighting conditions prompted Boeing to undertake a redesign of the system. The aircraft has also experienced difficulties involving its refuelling boom.

The programme’s fixed-price development contract has left Boeing absorbing billions of dollars in additional costs.

Despite these setbacks, the US Air Force has progressively expanded its use of the Pegasus in training, overseas deployments and operational missions.

Military orders extend the life of the Boeing 767

The additional tanker order is also significant for the future of Boeing’s 767 manufacturing operations at Everett, Washington.

As previously reported by AGN, Boeing is expected to conclude production of the commercial 767-300F freighter in 2027 ahead of the introduction of tighter international aircraft emissions requirements.

The 767 first flew in 1981 and became a widely used twin-engine widebody on domestic and international passenger routes.

Boeing delivered its final passenger 767-300ER in 2014 as airlines increasingly turned to newer aircraft, including the 787 Dreamliner.

Demand from cargo operators subsequently helped sustain production, with FedEx and UPS among the principal customers for the factory-built 767 freighter.

However, Boeing has not developed a freighter version of the 787, leaving it without a direct replacement for the 767-300F in the same market segment.

Military production will continue beyond the commercial manufacturing deadline.

The KC-46A is derived from the 767-200ER, incorporating elements of the 767 freighter’s design, reinforced structures, military communications equipment and cockpit technology developed for the 787 Dreamliner.

The tanker can carry approximately 212,000lb (96,160kg) of fuel and is powered by two Pratt & Whitney PW4062 engines.

It can refuel aircraft using both flying-boom and probe-and-drogue systems, allowing it to support a wide range of US and allied military aircraft.

The Pegasus can also be configured to carry passengers, cargo and patients requiring aeromedical evacuation.

Growing operational role for the KC-46A

Boeing highlighted recent KC-46A missions supporting humanitarian assistance, including the transportation of relief supplies under the US government’s Denton Humanitarian Assistance Program.

The aircraft has also participated in bilateral training involving the US and Japanese air forces, while long-distance deployments from Travis Air Force Base in California to Japan have supported operations across the Pacific.

The US Air Force, meanwhile, faces the challenge of replacing hundreds of ageing KC-135s while determining what kind of tanker it will require in the coming decades.

]]> Plus Ultra suspends last remaining flights amid financial woes https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/plus-ultra-airline-cancels-flights/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 08:50:06 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57877 The decision on Monday by Plus Ultra, which has been operating for over a decade, saw the carrier axe its last remaining scheduled route from Madrid to Caracas in Venezuela.

The post Plus Ultra suspends last remaining flights amid financial woes appeared first on AGN.

]]> Spanish airline Plus Ultra Líneas Aéreas has suspended all flight operations with effect from 23 November, blaming unsuccessful efforts to secure a solution to its worsening financial position.

The decision on Monday by Plus Ultra, which has been operating for over a decade, saw the carrier axe its last remaining scheduled route from Madrid to Caracas in Venezuela.

Plus Ultra axes routes amid financial pressures

Plus Ultra has been gradually winding back its schedule. The carrier filed for creditor protection , closing its routes from Madrid to Lima and Buenos Aires last week.

Founded in Spain in 2015, Plus Ultra began scheduled long-haul operations in June 2016, specialising in routes between Madrid and destinations in Latin America and Africa. 

The airline operated an all-Airbus A330 fleet, offering scheduled passenger services alongside ACMI and charter operations, with a network including Bogotá, Cartagena, Caracas, Lima and Malabo.

The carrier announced the final suspension of flights saying its services would remain grounded until further notice as it continues to explore options under a wider restructuring process.

Airline pursued ‘intense negotiations’ before suspending operations

In a statement in Spanish, Plus Ultra said it had carried out a “period of intense negotiations” aimed at resolving its precarious financial position, but that they had failed to produce a solution. 

The airline said it was continuing to evaluate possible options to salvage its operation but had decided to halt flying in the meantime while those efforts continued.

Plus Ultra added in its statement that its priority was managing the situation in an “orderly manner while continuing to analyse the available options”.

A growing list of airline closures

Plus Ultra’s demise comes as a wave of airlines have faced similar issues amid high fuel prices and supply chain constraints. 

Slovakian ACMI and charter operator AirExplore announced earlier this month that it had ceased operations after 16 years.

The carrier officially stopped flying on 10 November and has submitted a request to surrender its Air Operator Certificate (AOC), bringing an end to a business that developed from a small Slovakian operator into an internationally recognised provider of aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance (ACMI) services.

Others include Global Airlines, whose operation was wound up by the High Court this month, signalling the end of a venture that flew just two return passenger flights.

The British startup set out with a bold ambition to “bring back the golden era of travel” with an all-Airbus A380 fleet, but which ended with compulsory liquidation.

Spain’s AlbaStar was another casualty, as was FLY4 Airlines.

]]> JSX to revive New Pacific Airlines, paving the way for 42-seat Embraer operations https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/jsx-new-pacific-airlines-erj145/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 19:49:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57864 The new arrangement with NPA would allow JSX to operate an Embraer fleet with 42 seats. It is currently capped at 30 seats under Part 135 rules.

The post JSX to revive New Pacific Airlines, paving the way for 42-seat Embraer operations appeared first on AGN.

]]>
US public charter operator JSX is planning to revive bankrupt New Pacific Airlines (NPA) under the JSX Air brand, with plans to launch a new operation using 42-seat Embraer ERJ145 regional jets.

In a filing submitted to the US Department of Transportation (DoT) on 20 November, NPA requested permission to resume operations under its existing air carrier certificate. It follows the acquisition by JSX of New Pacific Airlines, which was reportedly finalised in August.

JSX to operate as a Part 121 air carrier 

The proposed operation would see the company conduct public charter flights under Part 380 of the US Department of Transportation’s regulations, operating as a Part 121 air carrier. 

Services would initially concentrate on short-haul domestic routes of between approximately 200 and 300 nautical miles, with an emphasis on providing additional connections to smaller and mid-sized communities, the carrier said. 

NPA said the plan with JSX was to “provide passengers with a public charter jet experience at attainable fares, including personalised and attentive cabin service, business class legroom, complimentary snacks and drinks, and complimentary Starlink Wi-Fi”. 

It said the operation would be modelled on the proposition offered by its sister company, Delux Public Charter, which operates under the JSX brand.

Crucially, the new arrangement with NPA would allow JSX to operate an Embraer fleet with 42 seats. It is currently capped at 30 seats under Part 135 rules.

Bringing 42-seat Embraer ERJ145-LR into service

The carrier plans to introduce six Embraer ERJ145-LR aircraft during its first year of operations. The aircraft are already operated by Delux and would be transferred to NPA through dry leases once the carrier is nearly complete with its Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) certification review.

The DoT filing does not go into detail about initial routes for the new operation. 

However, NPA said it expects to expand its network over time, particularly to smaller and mid-sized cities. These are “communities that, in recent years, have seen declining levels of service from major scheduled airlines”, the filing stated. 

NPA is wholly owned by JetSuiteX, the parent company of JSX and Delux Public Charter. 

The company’s chief executive, Alex Wilcox, will also lead the revived airline. 

Read more: Heart Aerospace unveils evolved ES-36 as JSX converts options into orders Read more: Heart Aerospace unveils evolved ES-36 as JSX converts options into orders

How did NPA reach this point?

The move follows a turbulent period for NPA, formerly Northern Pacific Airways, which discontinued operations on 26 November 2025.

The carrier launched in 2022 with the express purpose of offering one-stop connections between North America and Asia using Boeing 757-200s with a stopover in Anchorage, Alaska.

Flights were planned from New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Orlando, and Las Vegas to Tokyo, Osaka, and Nagoya, Japan, as well as Seoul, South Korea.

In 2023, it was forced to change its name to New Pacific Airlines to avoid having to contest a trademark lawsuit.

The airline and several affiliates subsequently filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 26 January 2026, following mounting financial losses and unsuccessful attempts to restructure its debt outside court. 

The bankruptcy court approved a reorganisation plan on 18 August, under which JetSuiteX acquired the equity of New Pacific Airlines.

The new application sets out a first-year operating cost forecast of approximately $53.9m.

The company is seeking a waiver from the usual 45-day advance filing rule, arguing that it would allow NPA to offer “additional service to underserved communities and [bring] competition to a highly concentrated domestic airline industry” sooner than would otherwise be possible.

]]> NASA takes ownership of X-59 as quiet supersonic flight moves closer to reality https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/nasa-x-59-quiet-supersonic-aircraft/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 18:44:40 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57821 NASA has officially taken ownership of the X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft from Lockheed Martin, moving the Quesst mission closer to testing whether supersonic jets can fly over land without disruptive sonic booms.

The post NASA takes ownership of X-59 as quiet supersonic flight moves closer to reality appeared first on AGN.

]]> NASA has officially taken ownership of the X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft from Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, marking another step in a programme that could eventually allow commercial passenger aircraft to fly faster than the speed of sound over land.

The transfer took place on 18 November and was announced by NASA on Monday, 23 November, following an aircraft acceptance review. Lockheed Martin will continue to provide technical support when required.

The aircraft has spent much of the past year demonstrating its flying qualities at different speeds and altitudes. NASA is now preparing for a more important part of the programme that of establishing whether the X-59 can consistently fly at supersonic speeds without producing the loud sonic booms that have restricted commercial operations over land for decades.

“To someone outside the flight test, this might seem like a subtle change,” said Cathy Bahm, NASA’s Low Boom Flight Demonstrator project manager.

“But for NASA, this is another big moment for the X-59, showing how far we have come, how much our hard work has paid off, and how much closer we are to providing the data to hopefully make commercial supersonic flight over land a reality,” Bahm said.

From 230mph to Mach 1.53 in a year

The X-59 made its maiden flight on 28 October 2025, taking off from Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works facility in Palmdale, California, and landing at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, which has since served as its operational base.

During that 67-minute flight, the aircraft reached 12,000ft and a speed of 230mph. The priority was to establish that its basic systems worked correctly and that the aircraft could be flown safely.

Following a scheduled maintenance period, the X-59 returned to the skies in March 2026. Engineers began gradually increasing its speed and altitude, studying how the aircraft behaved under different aerodynamic conditions.

On 5 June, NASA test pilot Jim ‘Clue’ Less took the X-59 beyond the speed of sound for the first time. The 81-minute flight reached Mach 1.1 at 43,400ft.

Less recalled that there was little to indicate from inside the cockpit that the aircraft had broken the sound barrier.

“You know you are supersonic when gauges say you are supersonic. I didn’t feel anything,” he said.

An even more significant milestone followed on 12 June, when the X-59 reached Mach 1.4 at 55,000ft. These are the conditions under which NASA intends to conduct its future flights over populated areas.

The distinction is important. The aircraft had now demonstrated that it could operate at the speed and altitude around which its low-boom technology was designed.

By August, engineers had completed 25 flights. NASA reported that measurements of aircraft stability, handling characteristics and structural loads were consistent with predictions made during computer simulations and wind tunnel testing.

No unexpected aerodynamic instability or excessive vibration had been encountered at that stage.

The pace of testing also increased. In September, the aircraft completed six flights in three days.

By the first anniversary of its maiden flight, the X-59 had completed 41 sorties, exceeded 56,000ft and reached a maximum speed of Mach 1.53. Its longest flight had lasted 102 minutes.

Why the X-59 looks so different

The unusual appearance of the X-59 is central to what NASA is trying to achieve.

When an aircraft travels faster than sound, pressure disturbances created as it moves through the air form shock waves. These can merge as they travel towards the ground, producing the familiar loud sonic boom.

The boom is not simply a noise generated at the moment an aircraft breaks the sound barrier. It continues along its supersonic flight path, potentially affecting communities hundreds of kilometres apart.

The X-59’s elongated nose, slender fuselage and carefully positioned wings are designed to prevent these shock waves from combining into a powerful boom.

Its engine is mounted above the fuselage, helping to reduce the shock waves directed towards the ground.

The design has also presented some unusual engineering challenges. The aircraft’s long nose leaves the pilot without a conventional forward-facing windscreen. Instead, cameras and a high-resolution cockpit display provide a view of the airspace ahead through what NASA calls the eXternal Vision System.

At its intended cruising speed and altitude, NASA expects the sound reaching the ground to resemble a car door being closed about six metres away.

Whether the aircraft can consistently achieve that level of noise under real atmospheric conditions is what the forthcoming tests will establish.

Has the X-59 demonstrated quiet supersonic flight yet?

Not conclusively.
Although the X-59 has flown beyond the speed of sound on numerous occasions, its early supersonic flights were primarily concerned with aircraft performance and safety.

A conventional NASA F-15 research aircraft accompanied those flights, allowing engineers to monitor the X-59 in the air. However, the F-15’s own sonic booms masked whatever sound the experimental aircraft produced.

NASA will now increasingly focus on acoustic validation, conducting dedicated flights within the supersonic test range around Edwards Air Force Base in California.

Researchers will measure the pressure waves generated by the aircraft and the sound they produce on reaching the ground.
Atmospheric conditions, including temperature and wind, can influence how those waves travel. Engineers therefore need measurements from a range of flight conditions before taking the aircraft over populated areas.

The public will have a say

Perhaps the most unusual part of NASA’s Quesst mission is that its eventual success will depend partly on people who have nothing to do with aviation.

Once acoustic testing is sufficiently advanced, NASA plans to fly the X-59 over selected US communities and ask residents about the noise they experience.

A sound that appears acceptable to engineers examining instrument readings may be perceived differently by people going about their daily lives.

NASA will collect those responses and provide the findings to US and international aviation regulators. The intention is to give authorities enough scientific evidence to consider noise-based restrictions rather than blanket prohibitions on supersonic flight over land.

The programme is currently scheduled to run through 2029.

What it means for supersonic passenger travel

Noise restrictions were among the factors that limited Concorde’s commercial operations, confining most of its supersonic services to routes over the ocean.

Since Concorde’s retirement in 2003, no commercial supersonic passenger aircraft has entered service.

Removing or substantially reducing the restrictions associated with sonic booms could open domestic and other overland routes to future supersonic airliners, potentially making them commercially attractive on a much wider network.

The X-59 itself is a single-seat research aircraft and will never carry paying passengers.

NASA intends to make the research, engineering tools and validated design methods developed through Quesst available to help manufacturers design quieter supersonic aircraft of their own.

]]> Who owns space? The treaties, laws and disputes shaping the new lunar economy https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/who-owns-space/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:21:46 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56140 No country can claim ownership of the Moon or outer space under international law. But as governments and private companies plan long-term lunar operations, questions over mining, territory and access are becoming increasingly important.

The post Who owns space? The treaties, laws and disputes shaping the new lunar economy appeared first on AGN.

]]> Who owns space? The short answer is no one; the long answer is considerably more nuanced.

As the United States, China and other countries pursue ambitious plans for the Moon, old space treaties are being tested by new technologies, commercial interests and growing competition.

Where does airspace end and space begin?

Article 1 of the 1944 Chicago Convention says every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory.

But a wrinkle is that the exact altitude at which airspace ends and outer space begins has never been formally agreed. The 100-kilometre Kármán line is widely used as a practical boundary, but it is not universally established in international law.

SpaceX’s Starlink satellites operate well above this, starting at 330 kilometres, while the 2023 Chinese spy balloon – shot down by the US – was flying at around 18km.

In practice, there is little disagreement about objects operating at aircraft altitudes or in orbit. The areas in between remain less clearly defined.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty: Why no country can own the Moon

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty remains the cornerstone of international space law.

Article II states, “Outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means.”

In simple terms, no country can claim part of the Moon as its own territory. However, how some aspects of the treaty should be applied to future lunar settlements and resource extraction remains the subject of debate.

The treaty also establishes several other key principles. Outer space is free for exploration and use by all states, and countries cannot claim sovereignty over the Moon or other celestial bodies.

Nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction cannot be placed in orbit or stationed in outer space. Military bases and weapons testing are also prohibited on the Moon and other celestial bodies.

What can countries own in space?

While countries cannot own parts of the Moon, they do retain jurisdiction over their own spacecraft, satellites and other registered space equipment.

Think of it this way: a country cannot own a piece of the Moon, but it does own the lunar lander, rover or habitat it places there. This raises important questions for future lunar missions.

If one country builds a base on the Moon, can another country’s astronauts simply land beside it? Can they enter it? How close is too close?

In 2020, the United States and seven initial partner countries introduced the Artemis Accords to attempt to forge an agreement to establish common interpretations and practices of the Outer Space Treaty.

The accords have since attracted dozens of signatories, although major space powers including China remain outside the framework. Supporters argue the accords provide useful operational guidance, while critics say some provisions will ultimately require broader international agreement.

One of the most closely watched concepts within the accords is the idea of “safety zones” around lunar activities, intended to prevent harmful interference between operators.

Supporters say these zones would help prevent accidents and interference between missions. Critics worry they could eventually be used to create de facto control over valuable areas of the Moon.

Can anyone mine the Moon?

Commercial companies, including Blue Origin and SpaceX, have expressed ambitions to develop lunar infrastructure and exploit extra-terrestrial resources.

NASA’s Artemis programme and China’s International Lunar Research Station initiative, developed with different international partners, both envisage sustained infrastructure on the Moon.

India is often overlooked, but also has increasingly ambitious lunar exploration plans. Its government has announced a goal of landing an Indian astronaut on the Moon by 2040.

The law about extracting resources is also unclear. Article 11 of the Moon Agreement 1979 says the Moon and its natural resources are the common heritage of mankind. It adds that installing buildings does not establish ownership.

The agreement also notes that states would agree to establish an international regime to govern the exploitation of lunar resources when it becomes feasible. That time appears to be approaching, but it hasn’t been agreed.

The American 2015 Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act recognises American citizens’ rights to own resources they recover from space, while explicitly disclaiming sovereignty over celestial bodies.

NASA uses drone to test autonomous Moon and Mars landing technology NASA uses drone to test autonomous Moon and Mars landing technology

Limits of international law

There are several reasons why uncertainty remains.

One is that the Moon Agreement attracted relatively few signatories compared with the Outer Space Treaty and does not include many of the world’s leading spacefaring nations.

Another is that many of the core space treaties were written decades before permanent lunar operations or commercial space-resource extraction appeared technically or economically realistic.

As a result, different countries sometimes interpret the rules in different ways – particularly on issues that barely existed when the treaties were negotiated. For example, Saudi Arabia ratified the Moon Agreement in 2012, but later withdrew, with its withdrawal taking effect in January 2024.

Even countries that have not signed the Outer Space Treaty are generally expected to follow some of its basic principles. Exactly which rules apply remains a matter of debate.

Lessons from other international agreements

A useful comparison is Antarctica. The Antarctic Treaty allows countries to carry out scientific research without settling long-running disputes over territorial claims.

Space is different because the Outer Space Treaty prohibits countries from claiming territory in the first place. Even so, both agreements show how international cooperation can continue despite disagreements over ownership and governance.

What happens next?

The basic principle at the heart of space law remains clear: no country owns the Moon. The more difficult questions concern what happens around that principle.

Who can use lunar resources? How will different countries operate in the same locations? What happens if two missions want access to the same area?

Those questions are becoming more urgent as governments and private companies move closer to sustained operations beyond Earth.

For now, the basic rules exist, but many of the details have yet to be worked out. As human activity on the Moon grows, pressure will likely increase for clearer international agreements on mining, safety zones and the operation of future lunar bases.

 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 /* 2026-11-08: bar moved from bright brand blue (#0056b3) to the navy the
 homepage redesign uses (#12233D), so header, hero and institutions band
 share one anchor colour. To revert, put #0056b3 / 0.15 back. */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #12233D;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {

 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}

.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.

 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {

}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}

#sie-lead-form-drawer,

 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;
